This paper details the development of a deep learning model for analyzing histopathology images, with a specific focus on detecting and segmenting complete egg shells within worm specimens. The primary challenge lies in the fact that the training and testing datasets originate from distinct laboratories, utilizing different microscopes, cameras, and lighting setups. Building a comprehensive dataset is difficult, as data is restricted to the specific institution that generated it; sharing sensitive institutional information is private, preventing the traditional approach of centralizing data for centralized model training. To address these restrictions, we have implemented a federated learning approach. This method enables the collaboration of multiple institutions by training the model in a decentralized manner, where institutional data remains on-site. Consequently, this ensures privacy preservation and promotes the sharing of knowledge across organizations. In our setup, an institution trains the local model using its own data, after which that model transmits the data to the central server. The server then synthesizes a global model by aggregating insights from all participating local models. This process repeats iteratively until either a predetermined number of communications are completed or both the completed local and aggregated global models are finalized. The results demonstrate that federated learning successfully yields a robust global model, effectively merging expertise from multiple institutions. This not only maintains data privacy but also creates a superior deep learning model compared to local models developed at single sites.

Identifying spatio-temporal anomalies in urban datasets is crucial for diverse domains, including predicting traffic disruptions and analyzing public health issues. Conventional approaches typically involve constructing specific data models that separate normal patterns from anomalies; however, this strategy is inherently limited, as prior knowledge of normality is often difficult to define. In this paper, we present a new deep learning technique that detects spatio-temporal anomalies by identifying inconsistencies between predicted and observed urban sensor data. Spatio-temporal Deep Embedding (ST-DE), a generative deep learning framework, learns efficient representations of spatial and temporal sensor data to produce reconstructed outputs that match real observations. An anomaly is flagged when the discrepancy between these reconstructions and actual input exceeds defined thresholds. We evaluate ST-DE across multiple datasets, including the TaxiLU dataset for lane detection and the New York City Yellow Taxi dataset for route tracking. Results demonstrate that ST-DE outperforms current leading techniques in accuracy. Furthermore, we examine the model's robustness under noisy conditions and highlight its practical utility for both offline data analysis and real-time monitoring systems.

This study presents a technique to isolate the vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) via all-sky stellar photometry, achieving precision within 5% of the standard satellite retrieval limits. While aerosol models offer good compatibility with observed data, they exhibit symmetrical modelled light curves that are anti-phased with the real, sky-specific light curves. We determine vertical AOD by fitting these optical depth values to the actual light curves, effectively removing the influence of the sky's continuous spectrum. A primary hurdle remains the determination of precise absolute sky brightness, a challenge addressed by integrating the model's geometric properties with measured stellar magnitudes. Communication bottlenecks represent a significant obstacle to the widespread adoption of Federated Learning. Recently introduced, Federated Distillation offers an efficient and decentralized method for sharing model knowledge by focusing communication on high-confidence prediction confidence. Building on this, we present Federative Distillation with Confidence Enhancement (FD2), a new scheme designed to accelerate model sharing at the edge by emphasizing high-confidence samples. We note that existing Federated Distillation frameworks often suffer from sample bias due to reliance on top-confident predictions and communicate excessively through frequent model updates. Addressing these issues, we propose a novel adaptive confidence amplification mechanism that leverages both per-layer and global model confidence scores to optimize communication efficiency. Experiments across image classification benchmarks and real-world mobile datasets demonstrate that FD2 not only reduces communication costs but also yields superior predictive accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art federated learning and distillation approaches.

Current multi-objective optimization approaches typically rely on a fixed utility function, derived from a single preference or a small set of expert insights, or adopt a formal model of the optimization problem. However, in numerous real-world scenarios, expert preferences are difficult to elicit, existing data is insufficient to train a reliable model, or no clear model exists altogether. Even when preferences are initially provided, their relevance can shift over time. These challenges make the Need-to-Know-less (N2L) approach promising; it defines the problem through a population of high-performing candidates and interacts with experts via targeted queries. This interaction can progress from individual preference checks for specific solutions to broader queries about pairwise comparisons between solution subsets. In this paper, we introduce a new interaction protocol, Pairwise Subset Preference, which queries the expert on comparing two groups of solutions. We evaluate this method against both pairwise and subset preference protocols and discover that it significantly cuts down the number of required expert interactions while delivering superior optimization results.

Recent studies have demonstrated that reinforcement learning (RL) agents remain vulnerable to adversarially perturbed inputs. This paper introduces two novel attack types: multi-step and distance-constrained threats. The multi-step approach exploits the fact that an adversary can perturb an agent's observations at multiple consecutive time frames, while the distance-constrained attack limits perturbation sizes. Notably, our distance-constrained framework encompasses multiple existing attacks as special cases. We comprehensively evaluate the distance-constrained attack across three agent families—Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), policy gradient methods, and evolutionary strategies—and demonstrate its efficacy in inducing errors. Furthermore, we propose a robust attack strategy capable of rendering RL agents completely ineffective. These findings suggest that current literature largely overlooks longer temporal sequences and provide compelling evidence that enhancing RL robustness requires simultaneous improvements in model architecture, value function estimation, and training data.

This research investigates risk-sensitive reinforcement learning, specifically targeting non-stationary environments where reward distributions shift over time, a problem for which few literature exists. Because non-stationarity renders performance evaluation difficult, we introduce a performance metric grounded in the "variation budget"—a concept previously developed for loss-sensitive learning. This new metric proves useful not only in changing scenarios but also in entirely stationary contexts. Our proposed method, NES-OFVI, draws its inspiration from SAE-OFVI, adapting it for risk sensitivity by incorporating an exponential tilting technique within the Calvo-Vermerrn framework to account for risk aversion. By employing the variation budget, we can determine theoretical upper and lower bounds on the performance difference between our algorithm and that of an omniscient ideal agent who possesses perfect knowledge of environmental changes. These bounds enable the selection of an appropriate variation budget parameter, ensuring that our algorithm's performance remains within reasonable limits of that ideal. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our algorithm, applicable to both static and dynamic environments, outperforms existing risk-aware approaches.

Distributed machine learning (DML) across time-varying networks enables private, bandwidth-efficient model training by multiple clients but introduces challenges such as inconsistency, slow convergence, and lack of guaranteed optimality due to communication limitations and data heterogeneity. Recent efforts to ensure convergence often rely on additional assumptions regarding the clients' local objective functions, which increases algorithmic complexity. This paper presents a more simple, fully decentralized, adaptive DML algorithm that guarantees optimal convergence over dynamic networks without requiring extra assumptions about the client functions. Additionally, a recent paper by the same authors introduces a comparable algorithm with only linear wireless communication; the current work provides rigorous theoretical bounds on its linear convergence rate. Empirical results demonstrate that both the proposed linear and a newly developed quadratic communication version outperform state-of-the-art methods in convergence speed and efficiency.

This study presents an on-chip multi-grating apparatus designed to direct multiple laser beams and generate an optical dipole trap for single Rubidium atoms using a $1550\ \mathrm{nm}$ wavelength. The device integrates two gratings on a $500\ \mathrm{\mu m \times }500\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ square domain, routing the incident light into four beams that converge to form a $310 \times 310\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ square trap with a peak intensity of $1.5\ \mathrm{MW/cm^2}$. Despite the trap's substantial diameter, simulations indicate a dipole trapping force that remains linear across the entire cross-section, yielding a single-atom loading efficiency of $90\%$. Furthermore, this diffracted-triple-gating setup produces a trap with a significantly reduced vertical resonance frequency of $2\pi\times 31\ \mathrm{kHz}$; this enhancement arises from steeper trap edges, which are confirmed to be advantageous for increasing the capture volume while shrinking the axial resonance to facilitate the detection of single atoms trapped.

Domained across chemistry, biology, and materials science, an artificial neural network (ANN) design framework is increasingly utilized for creating new chemical compounds with tailored properties. To date, the standard workflow involves training the ANN on existing molecular data to forecast properties for unknown compounds. However, this conventional strategy often leads to exploration of chemical spaces already represented in the training dataset. To circumvent this bias, we propose design-and-train iterative framework where multiple generative models are guided by the trained ANNs, each of which then explores distinct regions within chemical landscapes. By learning from this framework, the resulting ANNs can effectively map latent variable distributions that correspond to target molecular landscapes, enabling exploration of chemically novel structures. In this paper, we apply the framework to a problem of molecular de novo design, where molecules need to be engineered with a predefined molecular weight. Through this approach we show that our method can generate molecules with desired molecular weight, which are structurally very different compared to molecules present in training data.

Dynamics-based optimization approaches frame continuous-time dynamic optimization problems as continuous-time optimization tasks. In scenarios where numerical integration is required because closed-form analytical solutions cannot be derived, this framework defines the system's optimal trajectory and control values. Notable methods under this umbrella, such as direct and indirect shooting techniques, involve discretizing a continuous problem into a solvable nonlinear program (NLP) or optimal control problem (OCP). This process generates both decision and free variables constrained by the system dynamics, which can then be solved using established solvers. In contrast, the Hamiltonian-based approach derives the optimal trajectory as an OCP seeking a solution consistent with specific optimality criteria, typically the Pontryagin Maximum Principle.

We investigate comprehensive Bayesian methods applied to high-dimensional linear regression by adopting data-driven empirical priors originally proposed by Scott and Berger (2020). These priors enable automatic hyperparameter selection and, under the proposed linear regression framework, circumvent the linear dependence between hyperparameters and dimensionality that typically necessitates manual tuning. Additionally, under specific mathematical conditions, the posterior distribution derived using this data-dependent prior is proven to be formally equivalent to a Gaussian posterior. This result reflects and extends previous work by Scott and Berger (2020) regarding multivariate regression scenarios.

This work investigates perturbative four-point amplitudes in type IIB string theory on T-fold backgrounds, which feature N=6 four-dimensional supersymmetry. The analysis focuses on non-orthonormal linear signatures, which give rise to characteristic symmetric groups as well as permutation and generator groups. These groups are explored to determine their implications for the theory's supersymmetry and dualities. We argue that the structural properties of these groups suggest a reduction of supersymmetry to N=4. Finally, this study assumes that these T-fold configurations correspond to a non-perturbative superpotential governing N=4 supersymmetry.

Investigating impurity behavior within strongly correlated systems, such as its spectral characteristics and transport properties, serves as a critical probe for understanding Mott insulators. This study focuses on a single dopant embedded in a two-dimensional square-lattice Mott insulator. We find that the dopant's motion is constrained, with mobility modulated by interactions. In the Mott insulating phase, the dopant moves a "small polaron," whose dressing carries opposite magnetic signs to the movement direction, resulting in magnetic costs for displacement. Using a method that self-consistently couples the motion of localized excitations with their surrounding cloud, we derive a quantitative relationship between the insulator's Mott temperature and the dopant's mobility. We validate these findings with a self-consistent, numerically accurate, and physically clear diagrammatic expansion of the dopant's Green's function. Notably, we introduce a numerically efficient self-energy formulation that spares the need to store or compute the full many-body wave function. Consequently, we can effectively model larger systems with higher computational efficiency.

Defined as advanced capability in two or more languages for both spoken and written communication, multilingualism frequently manifests through code-switching or code-mixing within individual sentences. This work reviews existing natural language processing (NLP) literature regarding its limitations and obstacles when addressing five critical social impact areas: crisis response, healthcare support, political engagement, anti-disinformation strategies, and hate speech mitigation in multilingual contexts. Furthermore, we introduce prospective datasets and models tailored for switch-mixed input and propose innovative research paths aimed at developing a novel multilingual social impact switch-mixed input specialized NLP framework.

Biomedical graphs, serving as versatile models for various biological complexities, have significantly deepened our understanding of health systems and accelerated progress in machine learning. Over recent years, significant advances have been made in extracting insights from these graphs through representation learning. This approach converts graph-structured data into low-dimensional vector embeddings, facilitating their use in downstream machine learning tasks. In our overview, we examine key representation learning strategies specific to graphs that are serving the biomedical field, assess their individual strengths and limitations, and illustrate practical applications. Finally, we explore the fundamental challenges remaining in representation learning and propose directions for future investigation.

Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), which are primary candidates for dark matter, may accumulate within dense stellar remnants such as white dwarfs. When these particles annihilate, a resulting burst of energy can preserve the white dwarf in violation of standard cooling expectations, classifying it as an anomalous object. This study calculates how long-lived, non-thermal annihilation energies would affect a white dwarf, proposing that they would increase the object's total brightness, or luminosity, by impeding heat loss. By imposing limits on residual anomalies based on observed white dwarfs, we derive a stricter constraint: any such particles would have to possess greater mass than previously thought allowed if they existed in energy ranges characteristic of current detectors.

Many individuals underestimate the privacy risks associated with uploading photos to the internet. This paper introduces the Graph Privacy Advisor, an application that acts as an image privacy classifier. It predicts privacy status by analyzing scene details and the number of objects present. To achieve better results with a simpler architecture, the system enhances the relevance of extracted image data. We identified the most pertinent visual features specifically for privacy classification, reducing the graph model's complexity by swapping high-dimensional feature vectors for more efficient lower-dimensional representations. Additionally, to address potential bias in prior information, the study models the distribution of objects within private and public images, followed by an in-depth evaluation of the introduced methods.

I develop a model of a quantum emitter situated in its own radiation field, employing a cutoff on past light cone to represent memory. This framework depicts entanglement between present emission and the caged recollection of its past. I examine entanglement from perspectives of both caged memory and uncaged light fields. My analysis reveals recombination as entanglement swapping, linking the current state with a memory having unitary, but non-locally determined, evolution. I argue that this geometry offers an intuitive model for explaining how a particle interacts with its own history, noting that delayed feedback from a classical oscillator shares similar entanglement properties. I also highlight that time-dilation provides a 'smearing' effect, acting as a smoothing function that induces decoherence. Consequently, I suggest an inherent connection between gravitational time dilation and decay processes in quantum mechanics.

Conducted at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ GeV and utilizing a data set corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 140$\, \text{fb}^{-1}$, the study examines the distribution of charged particles as a function of multiplicity, where particles are specified by their multiplicity, $z \, = \, p_{\text{T, particle}}/\, p_{\text{T, trigger}}$, and the transverse momentum, $p_{\text{T, particle}}$, relative to the entire system. Analysis focuses on events where the transverse momentum of the entire system exceeds 25 GeV, with the photon-tagged subset requiring a detected photon possessing $p_{\text{T, photon}} > 25$ GeV. By comparing these findings against predictions from PYTHIA 8 and HERWIG++ event generators, as well as EPPS16 and CT18 parton distribution functions, the research offers insights into fragmentation and hadronization mechanisms, as well as the modification of parton distribution functions within the forward region induced by a high-$p_{\text{T, photon}}$.

Solar atmospheric nanoflares are hypothesized to supply the heat sustaining a coronal thermal balance, although a direct observation of them remains elusive. An analysis of a high-resolution, high-cadence solar image dataset reveals an event with a spatial scale of approximately 100 km and energy output of roughly $10^{25}$ ergs, representing, to our knowledge, the smallest and lowest-energy flare ever detected. This observation indicates that at current technological capabilities, detecting individual nanoflare occurrences is improbable. Instead, future detectors must achieve the ability to resolve even greater numbers of events spanning the full range of coronal heating models to effectively build up to significant energy accumulations. Only then can scientists determine if the corona is warmed by numerous tiny flares.

Social influence prediction involves estimating an individual's likelihood of adopting an idea or product within a social context, often relying on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) which have proven effective. However, the demand for high-quality, large-scale labeled influence datasets is often unmet, prompting research into whether these networks can effectively transfer learning from one dataset to another. This study addresses this possibility, specifically examining potential performance enhancements from using auxiliary source data. By testing various graph neural architectures on the highly influential Challenge2 dataset, we evaluated the impact of augmenting it with three other challenge datasets, either by simply adding node and edge features or applying multi-objective optimization to a heterogeneous GNN. Our findings confirm that learning from multiple datasets consistently outperforms single-source training, with well-represented auxiliary data yielding the strongest incremental gains. While initial improvements were observed, further increases showed diminishing returns. To maximize efficacy, we also analyzed weight-sharing strategies when integrating auxiliary data. Ultimately, these multi-data approaches, when combined with features from prior Challenge2 winners, established new state-of-the-art performance.

This research establishes a theoretical framework for pose estimation utilizing total least squares on vector observations corrupted by noise. The observers are defined as mapping the estimated parameters to the residual observation error. By computing the standard errors of the resulting pose estimates, we determine their lower bound via the Cramér-Rao lower bound. Furthermore, in a specific scenario where observation errors are negligible compared to the target's dimensions, we develop an approximate closed-form expression for this bound. This approximation is validated against Monte Carlo simulations. Notably, our proposed approach is significantly more computationally efficient than traditional methods and offers superior accuracy relative to the standard Jacobian-based linearization used in the YStein estimator.

Models are proposed in which a cosmological dark matter model is provided by a pair of complex scalar fields belonging to a hidden sector that exhibits $U(1)$ symmetry under a global transformation. This unique setup generates two distinct types of dark matter, complex conjugate of each other, separated by the potential barrier of the scalar potential. Various mechanisms for potential barrier crossing are explored, including a model in which a dark matter annihilation channel is enhanced by coupling the barrier field to the standard model, specifically its $Higgs$ boson. Different production mechanisms are analyzed to determine the abundance of hidden sector dark matter, covering scenarios with spontaneous symmetry breaking as well as models with explicit global $U(1)$ symmetry. Furthermore, various phenomenological implications are examined, including constraints from the dark radiation, dark matter-photon coupling, and a model in which one component of dark matter acts as dark radiation.

This paper proposes an end-to-end deep learning framework for the "color-plus-mono" dual-camera system to merge monochrome and color images. Using the strengths of both a faster monochrome sensor (high quantum efficiency) and a slower color sensor (high color fidelity), monochrome images enable a larger number of frames to be captured, particularly in low light. By integrating data from color and monochrome cameras, the system achieves superior color accuracy, higher signal-to-noise ratio, and higher frame rates compared to single cameras. We employ a two-stage procedure: first, we align monochrome images to the color frame using a two-step phase-cancellation algorithm, and then we upsample monochrome content to fill gaps created by the color camera's limited framerate. We validate this methodology on real-world datasets, including a self-recorded one from our lab and publicly available "Traffic" footage from Xian, and we introduce "MakeUp," a new public dataset with synchronized dual sensors. Our code is freely available at https://github.com/zhengyuanx/color-plus-mono.

We investigate two recently proposed extensions involving the lensing consistency parameter, $A_L$, specifically the $w$CDM+A$_L$ and $\Lambda$wCDM+$_L$ models. These findings are based on extensive datasets including SNe Ia from Pantheon, BAO from RSD and clumpiness, CMB data from Planck, and H$_0$ estimates. Parameter estimates for the new models were derived using the latest Planck data ($2018$), alongside a detailed comparison against standard $\Lambda$wCDM and flat $\Lambda$CDM frameworks. Results indicate that the differential impact of $A_L$ varies between the two alternative equation-of-state descriptions. Notably, incorporating $A_L$ improves model performance in certain observational metrics when comparing the new class to standard $\Lambda$wCDM, although no substantial difference in statistical fit is detected across all data types relative to standard $\Lambda$wCDM. Furthermore, the inferred values of $H_0$ fall within observational ranges, effectively avoiding the "$H_0$ tension" associated with previous standard $\Lambda$wCDM findings.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has emerged as a promising approach to leverage information from auxiliary domains to enhance performance within data-sparse target domains. Nevertheless, existing models often struggle to effectively balance the influence of relevant auxiliary tasks, leading to suboptimal main task performance. Additionally, they frequently rely solely on the same domain for link propagation, causing them to miss valuable interaction potential. To address these limitations, we introduce MSDCR (Multi-Sparse-D Collaborative Domain), a Multi-Sparse-D Collaborative domain recommendation framework. MSDCR minimizes unnecessary information interference by establishing sparse links within multiple domains and simultaneously exploits the sparse links to propagate user preferences. The model is evaluated using two real-world datasets and comparative analyses reveal MSDCR's distinct advantages in handling interference and link density.

"In this study, we examine kink solitons arising from two-field scalar interaction systems that satisfy coupled first-order differential equations. Leveraging the method of inverse scattering integration, we establish that specific kink solutions rely on a null-solution to a non-linear, self-adjoint spectral problem reminiscent of the Time-Dependent Schr\"odinger equation (TDSE). Consequently, we derive a rigorous lower bound for the energy of arbitrary, time-dependent 2kink solitons, demonstrating that this bound restricts the potential energy of the first field, $s$, to a strip within the $s$-real axis and confines $v$, the second field, to y-bands. Finally, we construct a 2-kink multi-soliton solution by superimposing single solitons with distinct velocities, highlighting its suitability as a foundation for numerical simulations of more intricate solitonic configurations."

Robots employing inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn from real-world observations may encounter disruptive events, such as power failures, that introduce noise into the data. We term these disturbances "nuissances" since the robot cannot distinguish which observations result from the target policy and which are nuisances. While traditional IRL methods assume perfect observation fidelity, our work addresses the challenge of identifying and eliminating the influence of these confounding factors. We introduce a new algorithm that iteratively refines the estimation of the target policy by simultaneously modeling the nuisance observations and refining the IRL estimate. To accomplish this, we employ a structural constraint within a multi-agent game framework, where one agent represents the true policy and the other represents a collection of observations, ensuring that only non-nuisance data contributes to the generated policy estimate. This method is validated on both simulated robot arm scenarios and physical robots executing novel tasks.

We propose a two-phased deep reinforcement learning algorithm designed for resolving demanding control tasks. While deep learning has proven successful in various reinforcement learning contexts, it often struggles with sample inefficiency. To overcome this, we introduce an off-policy strategy. First, we describe a coarse exploration stage during which the off-policy network is trained on an environment with rough discretization, which generates initial, low-precision samples. Second, we introduce a fine-exploration phase where the on-policy network refines its performance using the high-efficiency samples produced by the coarse network. This hybrid approach enables the integration of both on- and off-policy techniques, resulting in a solution that is not only highly sample-efficient but also highly effective. Our system exhibits superior sample efficiency, stability, and success rates across various benchmarks, including high-dimensional states, sparse reward structures, and environments with irregular reward signals.

We introduce the first statistical analysis of supermassive black hole (SMBH) evolution within high-redshift star-forming galaxies, focusing on a sample of 111 luminous systems at $z=2.15$ belonging to the COSMOS field. Utilizing the estimated SMBH mass assembly timeline, we compare our findings against two primary accretion mechanisms: growth through gas dynamical contraction and feedback-driven collapse. Our results indicate that in galaxies with specific star formation rates ($\text{sSFR}$) exceeding $2.5 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{yr}^{-1}$, black hole evolution is primarily driven by initial conditions, as these objects likely reached their required masses before the epoch of $z=2.15$. Conversely, for most other systems in the sample, most black holes formed at or after $z=2.15$, necessitating a reliance on gas dynamical contraction to explain their final SMBH masses. This post-$z=2.15$ contraction likely resulted from the significant enhancement in core dynamical friction experienced by black holes during the contraction of their host galaxies.

Deep neural networks are increasingly employed to extract information from data in large-scale scientific projects like the LHC at CERN, which utilizes millions of neural networks across its experimental apparatus. However, issues such as parameter over-proliferation and network complexity often prevent their use in production environments, necessitating methods for targeted, efficient tuning. We introduce a novel strategy for optimizing multiple networks simultaneously by leveraging a shared optimization landscape, specifically through managing the architectures of deep neural networks. Additionally, we investigate the correlation between performance metrics, such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and optimization steps, analyzing these relationships to inform architectural decisions. We also describe a system, tested on a production-level dataset, that automates the tuning of deep neural network structures.

Preprints represent manuscripts of scientific research shared prior to formal journal publication, and they have recently grown exponentially since 1980. As of 2018, however, only 10% of all research articles in the arXiv database correspond to papers, despite this significant expansion. This work seeks to understand the dynamics of preprint adoption and acceptance, focusing on how these dynamics affect both the timing and probability of publication in traditional journals. Utilizing various statistical models, including multi-homogeneous multiple event rate models, we analyze a dataset comprising authorship, subject matter, citation counts, age, and turnover metrics. Our findings address four critical issues: (A) subject relevance is the dominant determinant of whether an article gets published in a journal; (B) subjects influence not just if publication occurs, but also when it happens; (C) articles in physics constitute the largest segment of submissions and preprints, yet mathematics and computer science fields show a lower likelihood of traditional journal publication; and (D) articles citing other preprints are more rapidly accepted by journals across all disciplines.

Robust research data management stands as a cornerstone of contemporary laboratory operations, a challenge that current tools address only partially. Traditionally, scientists have relied on disparate digital and physical formats for notes, creating fragmentation that impedes the preservation, recovery, and sharing of information. We introduce an electronic laboratory notebook (ELN) designed specifically for the lifecycle of deductive research within time-constrained academic environments. By offering a cost-effective, implementable, and open-source framework based on web technologies, our system leverages modular design and established libraries to ensure compatibility with current data standards. This flexibility facilitates adaptation and integration with other research tools. Further promoting interoperability, the system utilizes standard Web services for data interchange and incorporates basic business intelligence to visualize the connectivity of the research network. We have deployed this open-source software for over a decade, refining it through direct feedback and requirements from diverse user groups.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), defined as multi-component metallic systems, have attracted significant research attention in recent years due to their exceptional mechanical properties. Their complex chemical composition results in intricate relationships between composition and structure that traditional methods find difficult to optimize. However, high-throughput DFT calculations combined with machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful strategy for investigating and developing these materials. This approach offers two primary advantages: first, ML models accelerate physics-informed calculations by predicting results from thousands of DFT studies, allowing for rapid screening of novel HEAs. Second, ML can identify patterns in computational data to guide the discovery of fundamental principles governing HEAs. This review focuses on recent advancements in physics-based ML for HEAs, outlining current challenges and opportunities. It explores various models—including Gaussian process, neural networks, and kernel methods—and examines how they apply to predicting HEA formation and phase stability. Finally, the article proposes recommendations for future research in this domain.

Binary matrices are ubiquitous in science, particularly in fields like ecology and epidemiology. This paper examines swapping algorithms designed to privately sample such matrices, provided structural zeros are either absent or handled appropriately. We propose modified swapping algorithms that guarantee privacy regardless of the presence of structural zeros and prove these changes result in negligible reduction in efficacy.

Neural network research has largely focused on ideal real-valued weights, whereas quantized versions using integer weights remain underexplored. Signal recovery methods within the framework of compressed sensing have attracted significant attention over the past decade, particularly following the widespread adoption of sparse signal recovery in diverse applications. We introduce a method for reconstructing cell shapes and analyzing cell behaviors by combining the flexibility of signed distance function (SDF) level sets with the computational efficiency of voxel grids. While traditional voxelization offers simple storage, it lacks the resolution necessary for accurate biological simulation, and standard mesh reconstruction from SDF levels is too slow for the continuous time steps required by these simulations. Our approach defines a specialized SDF directly on the voxel lattice, where gradients are calculated exactly and curvature is approximated accurately using local values. To handle organelles and multicolor data, our model integrates additional voxel fields. Furthermore, we developed an efficient algorithm to transition between valid SDF shapes by optimizing specific functionals. Demonstrations involving synthetic data and actual microscopy images of migrating cells illustrate the model's flexibility in capturing complex morphologies and its suitability for scientific applications.

Neuroscience evidence and mathematical limitations of Cartesian space have prompted the exploration of alternative representations for spatial perception and navigation. This study introduces a comprehensive theoretical framework for a potential hyper-geometric model. We explore how the brain could learn to embed high-dimensional, continuous visual scenes while preserving geometric structures through experience. Our theory aligns with neural processing steps observed in primate brains and can be integrated into autonomous navigation systems. We demonstrate the model's capabilities in two key areas: (1) learning a place representation that maintains spatial coherence across an agent's trajectory through simulated environments; and (2) generating distinct grid-like patterns when the agent navigates two-dimensional physical layouts. These capabilities position the proposed model as a robust foundation for future advancements in spatial perception and navigation research.

This study benchmarks event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithms against the standard local reversible Metropolis algorithm when simulating hard spheres. Our results indicate that non-reversible ECMC methods achieve significantly faster convergence for the hard-sphere system compared to reversible Metropolis algorithms, achieving this with integration over smaller sample spaces. We further demonstrate that ECMC's exceptional statistical efficiency stems from its computation of equilibrium properties along a deterministic trajectory, eliminating the need to generate independent configurations. This observation supports the conclusion that ECMC evaluates the equilibrium distribution over highly correlated trajectories, and suggests that other systems might yield optimal computational efficiency when trajectories are sufficiently tight, minimizing noise while preserving strong correlations.

Spectra of random matrices constitute real lines within the complex plane constituting the zeros of Gaussian analytic functions. Although these spectral zero sets exhibit significant structure that theoretically complicates rigorous analysis—specifically because they are irregular yet closely aligned with high-dimensional geometry and possess quasi-deterministic structures despite inheriting randomness from analytic definitions—their behavior allows for the construction of approximating processes with bounded variance. This paper introduces a novel class of multichimera states within networks of phase oscillators. Unlike standard singlechimera states that feature a single coexistence zone of synchronized and desynchronized regions, these new states exhibit multiple distinct domains of desynchronization. We provide a sufficient condition for the emergence of these states in general topologies. Our findings indicate that such states are resilient to minor perturbations in parameter values. Furthermore, we demonstrate that regions of multichimera attraction can intersect, forming attraction domains with intricate, fractal-like boundaries. A direct consequence of these intersections is sensitive dependence on initial conditions, leading to intricate dynamical outcomes. Additionally, we examine how these multistates transition into synchronization as desynchronization fades at specific critical threshold values.

Quantum science primarily focuses on manipulating matter's quantum characteristics through precise control techniques, which are essential for applications such as quantum computing, communication, and sensing technology. Quantum control theory underpins these advancements by developing methods to steer quantum systems from an initial to a specific target state. While early research centered on open-loop control designed to drive systems along predetermined trajectories, modern advancements favor closed-loop systems that utilize measurement-based corrections to reduce errors caused by noise and deviations, thereby enhancing robustness. Nevertheless, practical quantum technologies often struggle with measurement inaccuracies, calibration errors, and operation times that exceed coherent durations, preventing effective utilization of traditional measurement-feedback loops. This paper presents a theoretical framework analyzing the feasibility of feedforward within quantum systems, demonstrating that while standard feedback is hindered by slow update rates and latency inherent in measurement and processing delays, feedforward can be effectively implemented if a unitary correction operation is employed. The discussion further examines how feedforward performance is constrained by the measurement basis selected during the initial step.

The proposed algorithm was tested on both fake data of two series and real-world on-shell cryptocurrency data to demonstrate its efficacy.

Terahertz radiation enables the selective tuning of vibrations within molecules and crystal lattices, revealing how the circular paths taken by ions generate inertial influences on electrons that parallel the classical concepts of Coriolis and centrifugal forces. These analogs include spin-rotation coupling and several forms of field-coupling or redshift effects, which can endure for multiple picoseconds depending on phonon dissipation. Enhancing the magnitude of these phenomena positions this approach as a highly promising avenue for using vibrations to manipulate specific quantum states, with implications spanning from fundamental theory to applications in quantum computing.

Existing research primarily focuses on enhancing CLE-THROUGH RATE (CTR) prediction by leveraging additional ad features; however, new advertisements often lack these details. In this study, we examine how leveraging information from similar, established ads can improve CTR predictions for newcomers. To achieve this, we propose a novel similarity-based CTR prediction framework. First, we employ an auto-encoder to uncover latent *ad characteristics* by compressing ad features. Next, we calculate the resemblance between a given ad and others based on their distances within this latent space. Finally, we integrate the CTR history of adjacent peers to forecast the CTR. Extensive experiments conducted on a practical industry dataset demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art models.

Historically, business process management has focused on rigid, step-by-workflows, although in reality, business activities often contain both structured and unstructured components. Although current modeling techniques struggle with these variations, the paper introduces a new conceptual framework for holistically representing knowledge-intensive business processes. By leveraging a specific notation and supported through case studies, this approach accommodates both structured and unstructured workflow segments.

Offering meaningful privacy protection for users of location-based systems is exceptionally difficult, particularly whenever multiple nearby positions are tracked over brief intervals. Previous k-anonymity approaches attempt to address this by returning a set of K distinct genuine destinations; however, these systems fail to provide adequate cover because the evidence required to identify which truth corresponds to which provided option remains within the revealed dataset. To mitigate this risk, we introduce a new k-anonymity framework that incorporates plausible dummy destinations alongside real user truths. Our solution also provides measures of differential privacy, quantifying protection by replacing users with options drawn from a broader population dataset. Our research includes a rigorous theoretical analysis of both data utility and the magnitude of plausible differential privacy attacks, along with an empirical evaluation comparing our method against current state-of-the-art systems using a dataset of approximately 11 million points.

Resting-state fMRI research is increasingly pursuing multisite designs to expedite recruitment and lower expenses; however, these studies frequently document discrepancies in functional connectivity patterns across locations. While analytical methods for multisite fMRI data exist, they rarely evaluate the efficiency gains these methods provide. This study estimates the detection power of group mean tests at the edge density level for two-group comparisons using data from the Oxford Multi-site Multi-Modality Imaging Brain Connectivity project, which involved 300 healthy participants scanned across three sites. We focused on power to identify differences in mean connectivity values. Results indicated that across various thresholding strategies, the study's design conferred a 30–40% increase in power relative to a single-site design with an equivalent effective sample size of N=100 per group, thereby confirming that the aggregate power surpasses that of any individual site. In prior research, the authors presented a Lin-Lu-Yau style Ricci curvature for directed graphs, aligned with the Chung Laplacian framework. The goal of this paper is to establish a characterization akin to that of von Renesse and Sturm, demonstrating our lower Ricci curvature bound through a heat semigroup's gradient estimate and a corresponding transportation inequality during heat diffusion. A key outcome of this effort is proving a concentration of measure result for directed graphs exhibiting positive Ricci curvature.

Recently, Natural Language Processing for Code-Swapper (CM) texts has seen advancements, largely driven by the use of pre-trained word embeddings and skip-gram models. However, existing literature offers limited analysis on how to most effectively train these models for code-mixing (CM) languages. This work investigates key hyperparameters required to build optimal Context Memory (CM) word embeddings. Findings from our experiment suggest that the best performance is achieved by training the model exclusively on monolingual (single-language) data sets rather than mixing multiple languages in training. We also conducted a comparative analysis between CM and non-CM (non-CM) languages to explore characteristic differences. Ultimately, we offer practical insights into constructing CM word embeddings and plan to release our pre-trained vectors for public use.

Density functional calculations combined with the first-principles Maxwell-Cornell method were employed to investigate how energy-range cutoff parameters influence the pressure-dependent evolution of the critical temperature ($T_{c}$) and isoscalas in H$_{3}$S. Results indicate that $T_{c}$ within H$_{3}$S is largely insensitive to pressure changes, despite a significant reduction in Fermi level density of states (N($E_{F}$)) as pressure rises; this occurs because $N(E_{F})$ depends on both the electronic structure and the shape of the electronic band, rather than solely on lattice contraction. Specifically, the mid-band N($E_{F}$) increases with pressure due to the concentration of electronic states, outweighing the effects of high-frequency phonon mode hardening. Furthermore, it was determined that mid-band energy-range cutoff parameters play a dominant role in determining $T_{c}$ and isoscalas, as high-frequency electrons and phonons contribute minimally to the critical behavior in this system.

We introduce **MEX** (**M**ethod for **E**xplaining predictions in **G**enetics), a framework designed to explore *which* and *how many* variants contribute to polygenic risk scores. Current *in silico* methods typically assume *only* causal loci influence these scores, yet they often *fail* to account for spurious associations arising from genetic linkage with causal sites or genetic pleiotropy, leading to biased results. To overcome these limitations, MEX applies **L1 and L2 regularization techniques** that impose penalties on *both* causal and non-causal loci during the modeling process. *In* silico evaluations demonstrate that MEX excels in identifying the specific number of relevant loci and accurately estimating their individual effects. *Furthermore*, the approach was tested using *exome-wide* data from *I*BD patients, where it successfully pinpointed *known* causal loci. *The* software is *accessible* at **https://github.com/CMU-ALETHIO/MEX**.

This paper outlines our approach to designing energy-efficient walking for thruster-assisted bipedal robots. Our method relies on walking patterns generated through optimization, which utilize periodic trajectories for the robot's center of mass (COM) and legs, coupled with a steady-state limit-cycle dynamics model. We model these dynamics by separating the system into two phases: a free-phase, involving locomotion with thruster support, and a constraint-phase, involving leg interactions defined by collision dynamics. To optimize for efficiency, we employ a cost function that minimizes energy expenditure, quantified as the mean squared accelerations of the COM. Our results demonstrate that this optimization effectively minimizes swing speeds, leading to efficient walking strategies.

This study introduces a novel approach to visual relocalization that leverages 3D surfel maps. Our method generates an initial coarse re-localization estimate by performing a volume search, which is subsequently refined into a more accurate result utilizing a fine-scale 2-plane sweep technique. Experimental evaluations confirm that this technique achieves a mean absolute error of just 0.666 meters when re-localizing within scenes.

Federated learning (FL) offers a robust framework for distributed machine learning, ensuring enhanced data privacy by allowing models to be refined across multiple devices without exposing raw information. Nevertheless, real-world FL deployments frequently encounter data heterogeneity, aliasing to Non-IID distributions, alongside difficulties in labeling due to constraints such as workloads from third-party vendors or crowds. When labels are missing, reapplying label correction algorithms becomes problematic due to communication bottlenecks, while partially labeled datasets further complicate matters, often resulting in subpar learning outcomes. Addressing these obstacles, this paper introduces Supervised Pre-training for Federated Learning with Partial Labels (SFP-FL). The proposed approach utilizes self-supervised pre-training to manage uneven and partially annotated client datasets, thereby enhancing training efficacy. By integrating a novel mechanism that balances transfer learning with the costs of iterative communication, our method enables efficient training that respects client-specific constraints. Empirical evaluations on benchmark flennets—characterized by significant non-IID skew and substantial labeling gaps, including scenarios with entirely unlabeled tail classes—demonstrate that SFP-FL achieves substantial accuracy gains over current state-of-the-art techniques.

This orbital and rotational conversion likely drives a jet, given that such jet-launching mechanisms are well-established for magnetars. We examine this phenomenon by analyzing both jet activity and disk formation through a series of full general-relativistic numerical simulations. These simulations begin with jet injections and were conducted for two black hole-spin scenarios: aligned with or tilted relative to the orbital plane. Our results reveal that, in alignment with earlier research, a relativistic jet is successfully produced in every case. Furthermore, we track the evolution of the neutron star and its debris, showing that the debris stream is funneled and concentrated by the jet into the plane of the black hole's spin, promoting faster fragmentation. We also track the emergence of a massive accretion disk, noting that its growth accelerates more rapidly in the presence of a jet. The primary goal of this note is to determine the rate at which a conditioned process approximates a specific Q-process, based on appropriate properties of the process's quasi-stationary distribution. In contrast, we also demonstrate that when a conditioned process exhibits uniform convergence toward an irreducible Markov chain, its quasi-stationary distribution approximates that marginal distribution in a suitable manner.

This research investigates the optical binding within a dimer of dielectric particles positioned proximate to a graphene substrate. Employing an accurate electromagnetic approach, we calculate how surface plasmons excited on graphene profoundly modify the forces exerted by particle scattering, thereby playing a significant role in optical binding. The optical binding force is observed to be several orders of magnitude stronger with graphene than with standard metal substrates like gold, remaining strong across a broader spectral range. Furthermore, we demonstrate that plasmon excitons can be utilized to trap dielectric particles at specific equidistant locations. Notably, the sign of the binding force can be toggled between attraction and repulsion by adjusting the wavelength, offering potential applications in stabilizing particles for optical binding and trapping purposes.

This study addresses the issue of hospital admission delays in the Emergency Department (ED) by analyzing whether lengthening treatment time improves in-hospital admission rates for patients presenting with severe, life-threatening abdominal pain. We address these unobserved, unmeasurable factors by employing a Poisson count model with multiplicative random effects. We find that granting additional treatment time yields a lower likelihood of admission, suggesting a need to set appropriate waiting-time thresholds.

This study introduces a novel off-policy multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm designed for collaborative task execution, specifically targeting the convergence to an optimal Nash equilibrium. Central to our approach is the concept of the functional gradient, which serves as the functional derivative of an expected functional and allows for compact system characterization by reducing dimensions from the product of all state-action spaces to merely the aggregate state space. Leveraging this reduction, we derive the functional linearization, a tool for approximating functional values based on limited observations. These theoretical foundations facilitate the development of the Functional Functional Approximation Type Q Learning (FFATQ) algorithm. In FFATQ, both functional estimation and local policy refinement are congruently achieved through functional linearization and gradient descent. Our analysis confirms that FFATQ converges to an optimal Nash equilibrium within the functional framework, provided the step size is adequately small, with support from functional contraction properties. Additionally, we establish a functional policy improvement bound for FFATQ. To demonstrate practical efficacy, we apply FFATQ to a multi-agent swing-up task involving a planar pendulum, comparing its performance against existing methods.

The surge in popularity of crowdfunding has prompted significant scholarly research. However, existing literature primarily concentrates on identifying factors that influence individual backers, often overlooking funders' behaviors and their critical role in the ecosystem. This study examines the decision-making processes of funders to fill this knowledge gap. Employing a combined approach of qualitative and quantitative analysis, the study integrates questionnaires, in-depth interviews, and log data examination. Findings reveal that funders do not operate in a vacuum; rather, their choices are profoundly swayed by the activity of other funders. Consequently, this paper proposes a novel mathematical model to reframe the analysis of crowdfunding dynamics.

While machine learning offers advantages for detecting network attacks, designing such systems is difficult because of heterogeneous data sources and the evolving nature of attacks. Designing with varying data sources is challenging as each has its own labeling process, vocabulary, dimensionality, and structure. This paper introduces a new benchmark dataset and a neural network architecture to overcome these limitations. We examine five different encoding methods to merge features from multiple datasets and evaluate their efficacy. Our methods achieve better than 80% accuracy on average using three of our datasets.

Opto-task sequencing involves determining which task a robot should perform next, what the specific parameters are, and the timing for execution, all while adhering to precedence and resource constraints like shared tools or areas. This process is typically framed as a mixed-integer nonlinear optimization (MIONO) problem, but solving these MIONO problems in the context of real-time applications remains challenging. To address this, this paper introduces a method to linearize the MIONO problem specifically for discrete-time robotic optimization, transforming it into the more tractable Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) format, which allows for rapid solution processing. The methodology involves constructing a parameterized sequence of tasks based on anticipated future events and historical data, then solving the resulting time-dependent MILP to determine when specific tasks should start. This approach is validated through a case study of a collaborative system, specifically a beer-pouring setup, demonstrating its practical application.

A semiconductor-barrier interface of exceptional standard is critical for producing high-quality, reproducible quantum dots essential to quantum computing. Building a device within this work involves characterizing SiMOSFET Hall bars on isotopically purified Si substrates that utilize thermally grown, highly defect-free SiO₂ barriers. We demonstrate a SiO₂ interface mobility reaching $130\ \text{cm}^2/\text{V s}$, a level suitable for establishing a foundation in semiconductor qubit research. Additionally, we present initial evidence of motion spin states within the quantum dots, supported by detailed analysis of charge states via electrostatic forces.

This study examines synchronization within groups dynamics involving two varieties of oscillators—type 1 possessing a local ring topology and type 2 a local star topology—interconnected via networks classified by their structural symmetries. The analysis establishes sufficient conditions demonstrating that system interactions lead to asymptotic stability, where the $N$ oscillators partition into two synchronized clusters, each containing oscillators of a single type and sharing a distinct temporal evolution. Furthermore, the results encompass the scenario of cluster synchronization based on multiple symmetry types within the coupling framework. Distinctly, the proposed model generalizes prior research on local coupling by incorporating varying oscillator topologies and investigating how inter-group interactions facilitate the emergence of multiple synchronized clusters.

We investigate how cultural factors shape performance across video search tasks. Through case studies of video search behavior in Chinese and Spanish contexts, we identify a reduced relevance for English search terms compared to their native counterparts, which often yield less varied video results. Furthermore, we present the first cross-lingual video search query dataset, the Spanish-Rosenberg (SRS-RQ) set, comprising 230 paired queries and videos translated between Spanish and English. This dataset is being released for the initial exploration of single-to-multi query relevance mapping and translation query expansions.

To investigate supersymmetric monodromy defects within the critical Wess-Zumino model, we employ analytical bootstrap methods. In this framework, we formulate a set of constraints specific to the two-point correlation function of scalar operators arising from four-point functions, a limit dictated by the defect's conformal dimensions and spacely conformal dimensions. By integrating these constraints with the analytical properties of the bootstrap integral equation, we obtain more stringent limits on an individual conformal family's contribution to the two-point correlation function's scaling dimensions and anomalous shifts. We begin with the case of defects exhibiting fractional monodromy, then extend our study to more complex scenarios involving multiple such defects. Additionally, we examine how a scalar monodromy defect influences pointlike operator scaling dimensions and anomalous shifts in the model's chiral sector.

Wireless interference poses significant challenges to wireless networks, particularly in densely deployed scenarios. This paper addresses the impact of interference correlation, a frequently overlooked factor, on local delay within correlated Gaussian interference environments. Our findings reveal that delay increases with higher correlation, with more pronounced effects observed in dense networks, as a less severe assumption of independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) interference leads to delays that are more favorable. To provide clarity, we compare performance against i.i.d. cases and illustrate the impact of various correlation structures. Furthermore, we establish that local delay is upper-bounded by models previously developed for i.i.d. interference, with the gap between these cases depending on network density and the strength of interference correlation.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective at solving node classification tasks in graphs, yet they often struggle when facing a label deficit, a scenario that commonly arises in practical settings. Existing semi-supervised approaches typically handle this by employing pseudo-labeling to fictitiously expand the supervised dataset with synthetic graph data. These methods, however, often incur significant errors that propagate through the network, degrading model performance. To address this, the authors introduce a novel framework designed to mitigate such labeling mistakes even when scarce real labels are present. Core to this solution is the concept of pseudo-label uncertainty, which quantifies the confidence in generated labels by analyzing local model prediction variances and graph-based information. Leveraging this metric, the methodology achieves robust learning by providing a rigorous assessment of confidence in generated pseudo-labels where real examples are limited. Empirical results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that this approach substantially surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, exhibiting notable resilience against uncertain or erroneous data.

Accurate video understanding is crucial for human vision systems. Deep learning has emerged as a powerful framework for video recognition, leveraging feature learning to improve performance. However, standard approaches often focus on pixel-level analysis, resulting in computationally intensive operations and suboptimal accuracy given the intrinsic variability of video data. To address this, we introduce patchwise feature learning—a novel technique that extracts features from image segments (patches) to enhance recognition accuracy. This method includes a novel framework utilizing coordinate representation and learning-based anchor boxes to achieve robust location-awareness. Anarchic patch extraction combined with feature aggregation forms another core part of this approach, allowing features extracted from diverse sources to be adaptively combined. This study demonstrates that patchwise learning not only significantly reduces computation compared to pixel-level methods but also achieves superior performance across various benchmarks, including2D/3D action classification and magnification. Additionally, the model shows remarkable resilience to occlusion, reinforcing its potential for developing advanced video recognition systems.

This research explores the optimal joint resource allocation for maximizing information capacity in Mobile Data Networks employing Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT). To balance data transmission with energy replenishment efficiently, the proposed architecture integrates a cooperative mechanism where partners exchange information and energy. Specifically, the receiver extracts data from its signal while harvesting power from the transmitter, while simultaneously, it transmits its information link to the partner and projects harvested energy back to the link. Formulated as a non-convex optimization problem, the goal is to determine the ideal time allocation and power split within secure communication boundaries. An efficient algorithm leveraging geometric programming and successive convex approximation is developed to solve the problem, delivering near-optimal results that are both computationally fast and robust across diverse system settings.

This work offers a spin-dependent analysis of spin imbalanced dilute Fermi gases, utilizing contact interactions and multiple interaction orders. By integrating quantum field theory, we employ Fermi's Green function method to derive an analytical solution for the spin transition. We observe that, at a fixed spin imbalance, both spin-chromium and ferromagnetic phases can emerge upon cooling, with these phases appearing sequentially. It is also demonstrated that three phases can be generated through changes in interaction parameters at a set imbalance. In the context of a contact interaction, the spin-chromium phase corresponds to the standard spin-chromium case. We derived an analytical condition to determine the critical temperature above which both phases are forbidden. By using a three-dimensional graph, we mapped the regions where both phases can be achieved as functions of spin imbalance and Fermi gas parameters. The analysis further reveals that increasing spin imbalance significantly reduces the critical temperature for both phases. By comparing our findings with numerical data from other research, we confirm the stability of the spin-chromium phase in our model. The magnitude of this critical temperature is also confirmed to decrease as the spin value increases.

This study presents a generalized framework for analyzing systems involving parallel RLC circuits coupled to a mechanical oscillator, a standard yet frequently overlooked configuration in which the oscillator functions as a resonator. The proposed model offers multiple advantages, including the capability for direct coupling with optical fields and the implementation of cooling and amplification of mechanical motions. By expressing the $g_{\text{eff}}^{2}/\hbar\kappa\kappa_{\text{m}}$ product explicitly as a function of the circuit parameters (including capacitance, resistance, inductance), the authors establish conditions for achieving optimal optomechanical coupling. The paper further explores the distinct characteristics separating this RLC-based configuration from traditional setups and investigates the feasibility of utilizing this configuration for microwave-based cooling and reading of nanomechanical resonators. Notably, the study identifies a novel coupling regime in a cavity-less environment where the effective spring frequency is dictated by the RLC circuit rather than the mechanical oscillator. These findings rely on first-principle equations of motion for both field and matter operators, avoiding approximations regarding the weak coupling between them.

This work studies semi-classical orthogonal polynomials defined on $\mathbb{R}^+$ relative to the generalised Airy weight
\[
\omega(x;t,\lambda)=x^{\lambda}\exp\left(-\tfrac13x^3+tx\right),
\]
where $\lambda$ and $t$ are real parameters with $\lambda>-\tfrac12$. Our primary objective is to characterise the families of orthogonal polynomials associated with this weight and determine the corresponding orthogonality conditions. These families depend on an integer parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$ for $\lambda>\!-\frac12$, and they form distinct hierarchies. These air weights are particularly relevant for modelling phenomena in physics and probability, including random matrices edge statistics, Painlevé II processes, and random growth. This paper provides a detailed exploration of the mathematical properties of these families.

This study examines how simple, reactive rules can produce complex patterned motion when agents navigate near walls. Specifically, we demonstrate that a minimal system involving point agents moving at a constant speed with fixed field of view and distance constraints, reacting only to walls, is sufficient. This dynamic is captured by a two-dimensional ordinary differential equation, which, upon a bifurcation, gives rise to a stable limit cycle. By extending the model to perceive corners, we show that inside such structures, agents are locked into reactive behaviors that trap them in corners. We analyze the resulting motion by breaking it down into primitives—such as getting stuck or moving along an initial path—and defining these actions as states within a discrete-time system. This approach reveals that the discrete system behaves similarly to a directed loop. Finally, we map the motion traces within an unobstructed free-view corridor by employing a similar decomposition technique.

This article extends our prior research to develop chiral aspects of two-dimensional conformal field theory defined on globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifolds with non-trivial topology. The study focuses on specific non-cohomologous classes of trivial, semi-trivial, and non-trivial time structures. We explicitly compute and contrast these quantities for the cases of global hyperbolicity and the presence of fixed points in the isometric group of the time coordinate, particularly focusing on the so-called "time difference" and "conformal defect." A primary objective is to allude to the arithmetic properties, including the, of these values.

Laparoscopic surgery presents a restricted view due to the optical distorting effects of carbon dioxide desiccation, and this obstruction must be overcome to ensure patient safety. A desmoking approach is typically employed to clarify the surgeon's vision; however, this process consumes time and incurs additional costs. This paper introduces an image-processing technique that clarifies images in real-time, based on color color models, specifically targeting gaseous mist. By analyzing these clarified images, the system enables better interpretation by the operator, thereby allowing for clearer visualization of the surgical field and improving overall visibility.

This study presents the design and implementation of frequency-robust Mølmer–Sørensen gates for a linear trapped ion architecture, utilizing Gaussian amplitude modulation coupled with a fixed laser frequency. We chose an operating frequency that maximizes equilibrium in entanglement accumulation across all motional degrees of freedom to achieve strong tolerance against detuning errors, a capability maintained even in extended ion chains. This method was validated on a three-ion assembly, yielding a reduction of less than 1% from peak fidelity across a 20 kHz detuning band; its application to smaller groups of two ions offers comparable near-universal quality outcomes.

We employ ab initio molecular dynamics to investigate the structural phase transition in barium titanate, BaTiO$_3$, treating it initially in its ambient-phase paraelectric state. Using a "finite displacement" approach based on symmetry-adapted distortion modes, we define the structural environment for this phase. Subsequently, we utilize ab initio machine learning potentials—specifically, Ba$_8$B$_9$ and the "environmental" neural network (BNN) and "environmental" network (BNN), and the "environmental" network (BNN)—to train models on these datasets and evaluate their performance in predicting new configurations. We find that training sets generated from the distortion-modes approach yield superior results in identifying the energy- and force-based characteristics of paraelectric BaTiO$_3$ compared to alternative training strategies. Furthermore, while the BNN and "environmental" network (BNN) both perform well in paraelectric simulations, only the BNN accurately models the structural evolution into ferroelectric phases. Consequently, we propose the BNN as a robust tool for exploring parameter spaces and identifying novel phases in perovskite systems.

Multivariate functional data are characterized by curves or surfaces that evolve across dimensions and are subject to random projections or distortions, introducing significant complexity in their analysis. To address this, we introduce an unsupervised framework combining Gaussian random fields and Gaussian graphical models that offers both dimensionality reduction and structured multivariate dependency. The associated inference tasks—both marginal and conditional—are solved via the method of moments. Our contributions include novel solvers, including a constrained ADAGRAPHIC approach, enabling high scalability. Finally, we validate our approach through experiments on computer-generated benchmarks and analysis of real-world functional magnetic resonance imaging data.
