Particle physics research has long focused on the $\tau$ lepton, a stable point-like entity with a lifetime of approximately $3 \times 10^{-13}$ seconds. Evidence of new physics could emerge from $\tau$-related lepton flavor violation or the anomalous properties of its excited states. This text introduces a survey of $-\tau$ physics organized into four categories: its production and decay, $\tau$ spectroscopy, lepton flavor violation, and the search for phenomena beyond the Standard Model.

The paper analyzes atmospheric models used in climate and weather forecasting, highlighting essential initial conditions for atmospheric circulation. It identifies key criteria—specifically stability, convergence, and corner effects—that trigger cyclogenesis, a process attributed to the corner dynamics first described by E.M. Frenzy. Although often overlooked circulation features, this mechanism explains cycle formation aligned with coastlines. The study suggests that integration of this mechanism into numerical models enhances circulation simulation, offering improved strategies for coastal development and planning.

Standard practice for modelling extreme values involves initially transforming data so values above a high threshold conform to a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD), with its scale parameter ($\xi$) dependent on a finite lower bound. An alternative approach proposes using threshold-invariant extremes to estimate $\xi$, eliminating the need for data trimming and enhancing the efficiency of estimates from data analysis. This paper addresses how to obtain robust, invariant parameter estimates, focusing specifically on the scale parameter. We propose a robust method to estimate this scale parameter using a location-outlier model with $M_\alpha$ estimators for values exceeding a robustly selected high threshold. We provide robust methods to estimate both $M_\alpha$ and $\alpha_{\textup{out}}$ that are invariant to data shifts and propose a location-contaminated model for robust threshold selection. Empirical simulations confirm that the proposed method yields greater robustness and efficiency compared to the standard GPD approach for estimating the scale parameter. Additionally, the paper applies this procedure to estimate $\xi$ from real-world datasets representing annual daily rainfall maxima from Australia.

This paper investigates offline reinforcement learning in environments subjected to adversarial influences. The adversary modifies tuples from the data-collecting policy, excluding the addition of new information. Our objective is to learn an optimal offline policy despite the manipulation. The adversary possesses only non-causal knowledge of the environment's transition dynamics and reward signals, while being restricted in the computational complexity of their attacks relative to the offline learning budget. The study establishes performance lower and upper bounds, covering general function approximation settings. It is demonstrated that if the adversary controls only a fraction of the data, an optimization using a rich function class can still achieve an optimal policy. However, if the adversary dominates the data, the learning task becomes comparable to online learning. The authors present a proof-text-independent transition mark (*).

This paper establishes logarithmic convexity as a consequence of an observability estimate at a critical time step for 1-D hyperbolic diffusion systems with dynamic boundary conditions. Based on this result, it proves the exact and impulse controllability of impulsive heat models under dynamic boundary constraints. Furthermore, it derives explicit upper limits for the energy cost of impulse control. Towards our examination, it presents a constructive method to identify impulsive controls of minimum L² norm. Throughout study, it shows our findings extend applicable insights across the theoretical framework of degenerate diffusion systems with dynamic boundary constraints.

Although recognizing the significance of detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) samples is widely accepted, the community lacks consensus on their precise definition and the optimal OOD detection strategies. This work categorizes such instances into two classes: a semantic OOD, where an example is dissimilar to any training data in a semantic context, and an exemplar OOD, where an example is distinct from all specific training instances yet similar to the general OOD class. By benchmarking 23 existing detection algorithms on three datasets, we found that prevalent density-based methods fail to distinguish between these OOD types, whereas feature-based algorithms are effective at detecting exemplar OODs but struggle with semantic OODs. Furthermore, our evaluations reveal a fundamental trade-off between these two settings, where no single approach succeeds simultaneously. To address this, we propose a hybrid framework that integrates both semantic and exemplar detection metrics, achieving superior performance on all three tested datasets.

Recent research has successfully developed and fine-tuned various artificial molecular motors. A notable advancement in this domain is the all-electrical realization of these motors, where electric currents drive the systems across energy landscapes to achieve sustained rotation. In this study, instead of relying on external currents to manipulate the motor, we employ an all-optical approach to control its behavior. Our simulation results demonstrate that optical pulses not only induce continuous rotation but also allow for the regulation of rotational speed and direction. Specifically, three-stranded motors have been identified as optimal for this scheme, enabling the implementation of an all-optical ratchet mechanism.

Origin semantics for transducers were introduced in 2014; since then, numerous characterization and decidability results have contrasted sharply with classical semantics. This paper establishes a further decidability theorem with this goal: it is decidable whether a given transducer of an specific type can be reinterpreted as a function respect to origin semantics. Additionally, byintroducing a novel syntax called "functional transducers," this work demonstrates that fundamental problems such as equivalence, inclusion, and minimization are all decidable for these machines under origin semantics.

To investigate potential self-interactions of the Higgs boson, we propose searching for an excited vector state, designated $X$, within its decay products. Our findings indicate that no $X$ state resembling a tetraquark can exist below 2 GeV; consequently, $X$ cannot mediate Higgs self-coupling. We also outline a strategy to search for evidence of $X$ in the $\tau^+\tau^-$ final state.

This paper presents a measurement of the mixing-induced $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ in $\bar{B}^{*} \to D^{+} D^{-} K^{-}$ decays, utilizing data collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8, and 9 TeV across integrated luminosities ranging from 1 to 9 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. Decays involving final states with either charged or neutral properties were selected using vertexing and kinematic techniques; specifically, the charge-conjugate channel exhibits similar behavior. The observed value of $\phi_{s} = -0.040 \pm 0.042 \text{ (stat)} \pm 0.010 \text{ (sys)}$ rad aligns with the World Average and supports the SM prediction of $\phi_{s}^{\mathrm{SM}} = -0.035 \pm 0.017$ rad, with no significant evidence for $CP$ violation found at a confidence level of $3.0\sigma$.

Airborne viral transmission occurs through infected droplets released by symptomatic or asymptomatic individuals who breathe, cough, speak, or sing. In confined areas, a secondary recipient inhales these viral particles if the concentration of virus-carrying aerosols exceeds certain limits within the shared space. Such aerosols disperse based on airflow patterns driven by passive or forced convection. Passive convection arises from stratification of temperature and density, whereas forced convection results from fans or ventilation systems. Understanding and predicting viral spread necessitates a clear grasp of how these aerosols migrate within the air. This paper presents a mathematical analysis of transport involving both passive and forced convection. We adopt a mathematical model featuring convection-diffusion equations, which, under the assumption of negligible diffusive smoothing, reduce to an autonomous ordinary differential equation with distinct coefficients. This formulation, subject to an inward Dirichlet boundary condition, identifies that the migration of virus-laden air depends on temperature, viral load, and fan activity. Specifically, a threshold is established such that beyond this point, infection in the interior becomes inevitable.

Building upon recent experimental gamma-ray spectroscopy data and recent *ab initio* calculations regarding binding energies and charge radii for nuclei in the A=40 region within the fp shell, this study presents extensive large-scale shell-model analyses of $ eta$-properties in this domain. By incorporating the observed $ eta$-decay properties, we have refined model spaces, developed more accurate effective operators, and improved effective field theories. In this article, $ eta- ec$ properties are extensively discussed, with computed half-lives generally showing good alignment with experimental values. A comprehensive table summarizing $ eta- ec half-lives is provided, allowing for direct comparison across $ eta models, which facilitates further validation and contrast.

Double-sided auctions, prevalent in financial markets, facilitate matching demand with supply, with existing research primarily addressing single-quantity trades. This work generalizes double-sided auction models to accommodate requests involving multiple quantities and presents fully formalized matching algorithms backed by correctness proofs. The core problem involves efficiently finding all valid matches within an efficiency problem that remains computationally hard. To this extent, the authors introduce a reduction to the well-established maximum bipartite matching problem in graphs with edge weights, propose a solution using the Hungarian algorithm, and demonstrate that its application yields results with a maximum marginal per-unit cost. Extensive experiments validate the efficiency and scalability of the proposed approaches, concluding with a discussion on future applications.

We examined $F$-wave bottom mesons within the heavy quark effective framework, utilizing existing theoretical and experimental datasets to determine their masses. The analysis of decay widths was employed to derive upper limits for associated couplings. Additionally, Regge trajectories in planes of spin ($J$) and squared mass ($M^2$) were constructed for the predicted points, which align remarkably well with Regge lines. The present results offer valuable insights for future experimental investigations.

Following a brief hiatus, interest revived with a 2018 contribution by Ferenczi, Kent, and Montanelli introducing lines of superpolynomial growth, thereby broadening the scope. Current research in data-driven dynamical systems modeling primarily tackles three main obstacles: (1) relying on overly rigid categories of functions for system dynamics, (2 employing insufficient state variables to capture the system's memory, and (3) modeling systems that are open to data flows that fail to conserve mass. This work presents solutions for all three challenges through the application of neural operators and the generalized gradient layer within scalar conservation laws. These methods are demonstrated across three conservation law instances: the Burgers equation, the linear advection equation, and the modified KdV equation. Additionally, this study introduces a novel neural network approach capable of characterizing systems with an unknown minimal set of states. This method identifies an optimal functional form featuring a reduced number of states by optimizing a single neural network. To validate these findings, we compare our learned models against traditional autoencoders and variational inference techniques.

The relatedness network of chess openings serves as a potent instrument for personal development, enabling learners to explore more advanced variants by traversing paths of high associatedness. Relatedness, quantified as the similar performance of distinct but structurally comparable sequences during human play, acts as an optimal guidance mechanism. In this study, we construct such network using a dataset of 11.5 million openings from openingbook.org and apply advanced network metrics to suggest improvement paths. We demonstrate that these proposed routes effectively mirror expert players' actual opening repertoires. Additionally, we identify specific subgraphs or "communities" that correspond to distinct opening families; this classification is validated by confirming families' relatedness when examined by masters and grandmasters. Our relatedness models, built via deep neural networks analyzing move patterns, significantly surpass traditional statistical methods previously used for definition.

This study investigates key observational features of millisecond pulsars—including magnetic field strength, spin duration, and mass—and examines how they relate to the accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs. We specifically assess the white dwarf mass right before the pulsar forms and calculate resulting spin periods by modeling relativistic magnetized accretion flows from irregular streams. Through this approach, magnetized models successfully reproduce the magnetic fields and spin periods seen in millisecond pulsar populations, yielding distributions that match local observed data. Moreover, this white dwarf accretion framework explains the upper spin-corrected limit for millisecond pulsar masses, which lies near 1.6 solar masses. Finally, we suggest that the presence of irregularities in the irregular mass distribution of white dwarrets—likely stemming from gravitational instabilities within their white dwarf—may be the driving force behind the irregular spin-up spin-down transitions of millisecond pulsars.

This work outlines a method for generating "nonlocal" constants of motion within Lagrangian systems described by ordinary differential equations (ODEs). For dissipative systems that admit such a nonlocal constant, the authors establish estimates regarding solution behavior and estimate the conditions under which non-uniqueness or non-existence of solutions occurs. Finally, this framework is applied to specific cases within classical and relativistic mechanics, both field theories and mechanical systems.

Massive collections of free online 3D models, such as those in Blender's repository, are accessible for creative use. This paper introduces a novel method to recover 3D models via "air-doodling" using VR inputs. A novel algorithm analyzes the trajectory from air-doodling within Blender to select the most suitable 3D object from a large library. The study is significant as it offers an innovative approach to locating specific 3D models, potentially revolutionizing VR-interacted Blender usage for creative tasks. The paper also introduces a new dataset containing 500 diverse 3D models from the Blender repository to facilitate evaluation. Additionally, a human comparison test was conducted to benchmark the method against random selection and other baseline strategies.

The highly eccentric orbit of TRAPPIST-1e suggests past interactions with other bodies in its system. By modeling variations in stellar radiation caused by its eccentric path and accounting for potential tidal and dynamical fringing, we examine how these factors impact atmospheric chemistry and thermodynamics. We find that fluctuations in insolation, combined with frictional dissipations, alter the planet's temperature profile and chemical composition. While the migratory history of TRAPPIST-1e cannot be definitively established without precise measurements of its semi-major axis and eccentricity—particularly because current atmospheric models do not entirely reflect simulated physical outcomes—the specific non-equilibrium states predicted within its atmosphere could leave observable tracers. Distinguishing whether an atmosphere exists in equilibrium or a state of disequilibrium is therefore vital for exoplanets with eccentric trajectories like TRAPPIST-1e.

Equation of states of both isotropic and anisotropic types are examined; analysis reveals that an anisotropic factor lambda greater than 1 is required for compatibility. We investigate how to derive the leading-order extremality shifts caused by adding energy and charge asymptotically to a charged black hole. Additionally, we examine the changes in entropy within extremality deviations for various solutions. By aligning results with the Smarr relation and extremality variations, we reveal that extremality corrections are governed by an average condition for energy density, which generalizes the dominant energy constraint. This text-like condition relates the field's energy density to its rate of change in the radial direction, typically satisfied in scenarios involving static fields. We further analyze this average condition from a fundamental perspective, demonstrating its similarity to conditions found in the averaging problems of general energy constraints. As an application, we calculate the specific corrections to extremality for vector and scalar fields by utilizing this text-tyle condition.

Building on the concept that a central visual system supplies goal-oriented reinforcement learning (RL) with a learning signal, we introduce a novel architecture ending in a virtual "body-centered" representation of objectives. While this body-centric frame offers no inherent actionability, it concludes with a differentiator: driving forces generated from its goal, which are then mapped to the actual motor system. This research demonstrates its efficacy by training a simple RL agent to place actions within a universe queue using either direct physical parameters or body-derived force dynamics. Results indicate that input receiving force dynamics adapted from a body-centered goal formulation learn more rapidly and generate smoother trajectories. We posit these principles offer a plausible account for the existence of intrinsic drivers in nature and present an initial rationale for why such forces might take the shape observed in biological muscle arrangements.

We extend the three-dimensional Poincaré algebra to incorporate a colour symmetry factor, creating an associated graded algebra. This framework allows for both structure constants and structures within mixed grade components. Our consideration supports arbitrary Hermitian Lie groups as the basis for the colour factor. Generalizing known results from SU(2) up to current experimental energies, our model covers any Lie group with ranks greater than or equal to three. In addition, we derive generalizations of the three-dimensional Poincaré algebra's exponential map, covering both Abelian and non-Abelian scenarios, and apply these tools to construct transformed coordinates and momentum definitions based on group actions.

We present fresh parameterized algorithms for identifying upward planar drawings of directed acyclic graphs, where a drawing is defined as upward planar if and only if each edge traverses strictly from south to north. These approaches rely on solving specific subproblems related to branch-width and path-width.

Image-goal navigation challenges agents to reach an destination defined by an input image within a limited number of steps. Although current top-performing methods demonstrate effectiveness, they often fall short of human-like efficiency. We introduce MemoNav, a new framework that enhances sample efficiency and combines a long-term and short-term memory with an explicit map to guide an agent toward a target state in goal-directed navigation tasks. Long-term memory stores past observations and action histories, while short-term memory tracks recent movements and the agent's immediate position on the map to prevent redundant actions. Additionally, guided by this memory pair and the constructed topological map, the agent plans a current move by referencing stored historical actions. We evaluated MemoNav on standard navigation benchmarks, where it significantly outperformed existing approaches in sample efficiency, achieving performance at or beyond that of other algorithms using fewer training data instances or reaching higher performance levels in the same time.

To support emerging technologies like device-to-device communication and small cell systems, additional licensed spectrum is essential for future wireless networks. In this paper, we introduce a novel license auction framework designed to ensure fair allocation of spectrum among network operators, ensuring no single operator can monopolize the market. By utilizing maximum latency as our fairness metric, the algorithm guarantees a level of allocation equity. Additionally, each operator is tasked with optimizing their own revenue generation through intelligent investments in infrastructure, capacity, and spectral efficiency. Numerical analyses confirm the algorithm's convergence and demonstrate the network's improved performance through real-world data sets, alongside an investigation into how spectrum allocation impacts operator profits, total system capacity, and overall consumer data rates.

"This work introduces a overarching framework for analyzing the collective dynamics of $N$ interconnected systems undergoing specific affine transformations, interacting through arbitrary structures represented by hypergraphs. By adapting the graph-theoretic master stability functions (MSFs) and master instability functions (MIFs) concepts, we establish a corresponding set of hypergraph-based master functions capable of addressing synchronization regions within broader synchronization manifolds. Our primary achievement is the derivation of explicit, sufficient conditions that are both local and global in nature. Specifically, we establish local stability criteria based on linearization and establish explicit regions for asymptotic synchronization using hypergraph MSFs/MIFFs and Lyapunov methodology; these conditions apply regardless of whether the coupling topology is weighing or multis. Finally, we illustrate the practical applicability of our theory with specific numerical examples."

We examine operator growth in systems governed by Lie symmetry. The nested commutcommutativity structure dictated by the Lie algebra dictates the system's entanglement characteristics and the dimensionality of the operator support. We observe that, except for a few specific exceptions, growth ceases once the system approaches an entangled or high-dimensional threshold. Consequently, we construct an integrable model based on the $SU(2)$ Lie algebra that exhibits continuous operator growth and analyze its dynamics. Furthermore, we adapt standard algorithms typically employed to detect thermalization in many-body localized contexts to track and study the evolution of these systems.

This study examines the dynamics of brittle fracture in two-dimensional materials, utilizing Timoshenko beam theory to model fracture surfaces. We observe that brittle materials exhibit oscillatory instability when crack propagation velocity is high, revealing a link between these oscillations and mode I instability. Our analysis, which considers both inertial effects and energy dissipation, identifies a key distinction between 2D and 3D cracks: unlike their three-dimensional counterparts, the two-dimensional oscillatory trajectory is not necessarily planar. Furthermore, because the fracture surface in two dimensions possesses finite width, we determine that the characteristics of the crack surface itself critically impact the nature of brittle fracture dynamics in this mode.

We establish that computing the feedback capacity of a finite state channel involves polynomial complexity. This approach relies on reformulating the feedback capacity as the optimal value of a specific infinite-dimensional linear program. By applying standard linear programming techniques, we simultaneously demonstrate that the feedback capacity is easily verifiable and bounded, with its optimal solution sharing key characteristics with the solution to the underlying approximation problems. These findings also imply that determining whether the feedback capacity of a given finite state channel is rational is straightforward.

Superconductors based on La$_{3}$BiO$_{6}$ perovskites are known to be strong spin-orbit coupled systems. This study examines a one-dimensional superconducting chain within this material, focusing on the interaction between a Zeeman magnetic field and spin-orbit coupling. We observe that the three-dimensional bulk material exhibits strong pairing suppression due to the robust spin-orbit coupling, yet three distinct mechanisms can sustain one-dimensional superconductivity. We label these regimes as weak, intermediate, and strong RSO coupling based on the magnitude of the spin-orbit effect; in these regimes, superconductivity arises respectively from magnetic field pairing, the pairing of excited pairing channels, or the lowest-energy excited pairing channel. We propose that intermediate and strong RSO couplings represent a novel form of superconductivity driven by the pairing of spin-split bands. We further suggest that topological superconductivity can emerge in a superconducting chain from the RSO + Zeeman configuration. Additionally, applying a perpendicular component of the magnetic field is an effective strategy to restore superconductivity. Finally, these systems are accessible for investigation using a TDC circuit model.

We survey prominent rationales commonly cited in literature advocating for complex formalism while introducing additional persuasive arguments. This concise study seeks to reinforce the challenging task of clarifying the fundamental need for complex numbers in the framework of Quantum Mechanics.

Let a graph $G = (V, E)$ with $|V| \geq 2$. A subset $S \subset V$ is termed *resolving* if, for every pair of distinct vertices in $G$, there exists exactly one pair in $S$ that is closer to one of them than the other. A *resolving$-basis$ is defined as a resolving set that is minimal with the property that no proper subset is capable of resolving $G$. The quantity of vertices in a resolving$-basis$, identified as the maximum size among all possible resolving$-bases$ within a given graph, is known as its **metric dimension**.\

This work evaluates the effectiveness of coupling ozone and ultraviolet (UV) light in gas-phase reactors to oxidize pollutants in flue gases, specifically targeting the reduction of sulfur dioxide (SO₂) through numerical simulations of a continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR). Chemical kinetics were integrated into a radiation intensity distribution model generated by a five-point-sourced UV lamp; furthermore, grid convergence studies and optimization of discrete radiation sources were conducted. The analysis additionally examined how residence time and reactor dimensions influence SO₂ removal efficiencies. Ultimately, optimized reactor configurations and operational parameters were identified, demonstrating this study's aim to contribute valuable insights for optimizing industrial O₃-UV systems for flue gas cleaning and potential adaptation in other gaseous pollution control applications.

This paper introduces a scalable software suite designed for simulating neuromorphic computing systems, designed to leverage multicore processing resources. By parallelizing simulation tasks, the approach significantly enhances execution speed, and a detailed evaluation of the introduced methods is provided. Furthermore and related, this work explores the application of clustering algorithms to classify classes of problems that benefit from significant speedup. This classification assists in scheduling and load balancing, and several practical implications of the study are highlighted, along with recommendations for utilizing the results.

The deployment of Machine Learning in practice frequently necessitates handling uncertainty, yet standard Decision Trees fail to offer a suitable representation for probabilistic predictions. In contrast, Inductive Decision Trees (IDT) were developed specifically to model uncertainty by replacing deterministic threshold checks on continuous features with a policy that balances feature cost against the resulting prediction error. This approach also accommodates variable costs for different features. This work introduces a novel, efficient training algorithm named the Inductive Decision Tree with Backpressure (IDT-B). Practically, this variant outperforms existing methods in both speed and effectiveness. Specifically, IDT-B delivers up to a 3000× improvement over the original Inductive Decision Tree (IDT) in terms of execution time. When compared to the backpropagation-based Cost-Sensitive Decision Tree, IDT-B achieves substantial speed gains of up to a factor of 30. Empirically, IDT-B also delivers prediction accuracy comparable to, or better than, that of its counterparts across a spectrum of real-world datasets and application scenarios, as supported by our extensive experiments on a public repository (https://github.com/inductive-decision-trees/idt).

Time series analysis relies extensively on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) for similarity assessment and distance calculation. Nevertheless, this similarity may necessitate aligning two time series, a procedure notorious for being computationally expensive. Although several techniques have been devised to accelerate this process, they frequently struggle with length mismares and lack practicality. This research introduces EAPunewed DT W (EAPruned DT W), a novel approach that efficiently computes DT W by leveraging the elbow-based pruing method. This new algorithm derives its name from the concept and can dramatically reduce computation by initially identifying a significant portion of elastic alignment and calculating distances between corresponding elements. Furthermore, it extends the traditional elbow method by incorporating a new, more expressive metric and its performance surpasses that of other existing acceleration methods by an order of magnitude.

Testing is a critical component of software engineering, yet many undergraduate students struggle with comprehension. This study investigates two learning approaches: traditional instruction versus an inquiry-based method. We present the testing-learn-by-inquire, a specific inquiry-based curriculum designed to help students derive testing principles inductively from hands-on exercise experience, as opposed to learning deductively from formal definitions. Findings from a controlled study involving 177 participants indicate that students enrolled in the test-focused learning group not only achieved higher scores but also demonstrated greater satisfaction, engagement, and perceived effectiveness of the lesson, when compared to students in a traditional setting. These results suggest that an inquiry-based strategy is a powerful in-service training approach, capable of boosting test performance, satisfaction, and motivation among students who may have struggled in conventional classrooms.

Explainable AI has become a vital element for tackling real-world challenges involving transparency and reliability, though its current state of development varies significantly. This distinction depends largely on the specific context and the necessary level of explainability. In this paper, we provide a detailed examination of explainability within the context of content moderation. Additionally, we present the "PySEM" project—a comprehensive Python-based software suite that includes visual models and metrics for explaining content modulators. The visual models component of PySEM features a Content Modereration Schema (SEM), designed to clarify how machines learning algorithms and human annotators function together in the process. The metrics component offers a set of measures for assessing the quality of explainability. The paper concludes with an outlook on promising future directions for research in this domain.

This study details a search for dark matter particles analyzing the Z boson decay channels involving final states of $Z\to e^+e^-$ and $Z\to\mu^+\mu^-$ in association with missing transverse energy. The analysis, which utilizes $39.2\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC during 2015, 2016, and 2017 at a $\sqrt{s}=13$ GeV, investigates two production mechanisms: mono-$Z$ (arising from single vector-boson associated processes) and associated production ($Z\text{--}Z$, where one Z decays visibly). By imposing constraints on the invariant mass of the selected leptons, this research excludes, within the context of the simplified two-body decay model, cross sections exceeding $0.021$ to $1.04\,\text{pb}$ beyond the production type and particle mass, respectively, failing to observe any statistically significant evidence for the physics under investigation.

We propose new types of $k_\perp$-dependent functions. As opposed to the established Boer-Mulders function, our proposed functions relate to the correlated spatial alignment of parton spins, rather than their longitudinal alignment.

Compactly supported homeomorphisms on Tychonoff spaces form a group that can be defined by a collection of convergences. A Tychonoff space $X$ is said to be homeomorphically rigid (H-rigid) when the uniform topology and the topology of continuous convergence agree on the group of its compactly supported homeomorphets. In this work, we examine these structures, constructing a sequence of groups with varying properties. Specifically, we first identify groups that are compactly supported but fail to be freely generated. Next, we address a question posed by L. V. Shtel'man regarding H-rigid free groups; we provide examples with both countable and uncountable ranks. Finally, we determine which metric spaces admit H-rigid compactly supported free group topologies.

This paper investigates inference regarding the common intercepts and stochastic trends within multi-variable time series that exhibit non-stationarity and short-memory properties. Specifically, we present asymptotic theory for the initial $m$ eigenvalues and the associated projectors of a specific sample moment estimator. This estimator targets a restricted moment structure designed to account for $p_0$ unidentified common intercepts and $p_0$ unspecified common stochastic trends. The theoretical results concerning these eigenvalues, projectors, and the reduced moment itself are applicable even when the number of variables $M$ grows large. We demonstrate the practical application of this extended approach by employing it to estimate the dimensions of $p_0$ for $p_0 \leq 2$.

M51-1000+0000, a recently identified massive galaxy cluster, is the first to exhibit multiple multiply-lensed galaxies. Its lensing properties were analyzed using Hubble Space Telescope/WFC3 imaging combined with gravitational models that offer robust evidence for its status as the second strongest lens discovered within the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich sample. The study confirms the cluster's exceptional strength by applying seven distinct modeling strategies; all converge on a convergence peak of $\sim 0.60$. This value was cross-validated using external data from the S-Z effect derived from the Planck satellite. Ultimately, the cluster's ranking as a second-top-tier lensing object (second only to R1000 in M51-10000) underscores its value for probing physics beyond the Standard Model in a system with a mass exceeding $10^{15}$ solar masses.

Internet service providers (ISPs) often lack an incentive to maintain high network quality because rising content demand allows them to delay necessary capacity upgrades. Some content providers (CPs) have countered this by implementing profit-sharing deals that allocate a fraction of revenue to encourage quality service, yet the optimal distribution of this sharing remains unclear. This study presents a model of interaction between a CP and an ISP, where a profit-sharing agreement is proposed to boost the ISP's motivation for network care. This model incorporates a cyclic process: the CP first sets profit-sharing parameters, the ISP responds by choosing its network quality level, and finally, the content demand emerges. Based on these inputs, the ISP upgrades its infrastructure and the CP disburses payments. By analyzing the equilibrium where both parties adopt strategies to maximize their respective profits, we determine the allocation of revenue sharing. Our findings demonstrate that such agreements effectively enhance the ISP's focus on quality, leading to higher demand and improved network standards, while also increasing the content provider's overall earnings.

$\alpha$-attractor models hold great promise given the insights they offer for cosmological observations. However, their predictive power for making specific forecasts about future experiments remains ambiguous. We utilize the $\epsilon_{V}$-cutoff approach to analyze $\\xi$-attractor models with a linear approximation, demonstrating that even when truncated, these models retain their $\zeta$-attractor characteristics. Furthermore, we investigate how to generalize this cutoff technique to achieve an infinite-derivative action. We show that a few representative examples within this class can reproduce the behavior of the exponential inflaton potential. Finally, we investigate the physical pole singularities arising from the action and a recently proposed unitarity constraint on derivative couplings, and we assess the implications of this analysis for $\\xi$-attractor models.

We demonstrate that for any depicted measured foliation $F$ and strength $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a large class of quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifolds where the $F$-cusp is $\epsilon$-close in the Hausdorff topology (scaled by curvature) to $F$. Additionally, we construct a specific subclass of these manifolds such that the corresponding invariant measured foliations are independently selectable and come with arbitrary assigned measurements.

This study introduces a nonparametric methodology to estimate the density function of portfolio returns, assuming they share the same return distribution across correlated assets. A central element of this approach is a novel measure of similarity between portfolios, derived from the commonality in their return distribution functions; consequently, the density estimation task transforms into a nearest-neighbor problem. The study provides theoretical results regarding the convergence rate of the distance metric and proposes an efficient algorithm for computing pairwise distances, alongside methods for deriving portfolio weights. Additionally, the paper includes a comprehensive experimental evaluation comparing its performance against standard nonparametric estimation techniques.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a crucial point-of-care technique for identifying cardiac diseases through the detection of abnormal heart sounds known as murmurs. This study evaluates the performance of deep convolutional neural networks on the revised, publicly available MIT-Stanford HuBert human phoneme-free cardiac sound dataset. We introduce a multi-scale architecture tailored for classifying these acoustic signals. Our proposed method achieves a weighted average accuracy of 0.86 on this dataset, representing a significant improvement over a baseline model.

For considerable time, Pontes has served as a pivotal hub in Havana, functioning as a strategic space that advocates for diversity and inclusion within Havana's educational environment and beyond. Although Pontes hosts numerous workshops, seminars, and collaborative initiatives, formal writing has remained scarce. Existing materials offer various definitions of key concepts such as anti-deficit perspectives, ableism, cultural competency, able justice, equity, equity-based approaches. These concepts are essential for fostering diversity in education; however, they are frequently misused, undertheorized, or poorly understood. Given this scarcity, there is a pressing need to produce accurate and precise written materials regarding these ideas specifically for Havana contexts.

Many institutions in the US and Europe have made significant progress in integrating these notions into their academic systems. In contrast, progress in Pontes seems limited. Based on observations from U.S. and European institutions adopting these principles in their academic environments, there appears to be stagnation in their application here in Havana. This essay proposes the adoption of an equity-deficit or equity-centered strategy as a viable alternative to remediation methods aimed at increasing diversity in Pontes's educational environment.

This work investigates the $\delta$-operator defined within a quaternionic setting. First, it establishes the existence and boundedness of this operator acting from the space of functions, $H^p(\mathbb{T})$, to the sequence space, $\ell^q(\mathbb{Z})$, specifying the required constraints on the exponents $p, q, \delta,$ and $\rho$. Next, it derives sharp norm estimates for the operator, expressing a bound in terms of the $A_\mathfrak{r}$ constant of the associated weight. Finally, it demonstrates that, when viewed as mapping between appropriate Sobolev spaces, the operator is complete, compact, and is congruent to a unitary operator.

This paper presents an experimental examination of bid shading within credit and non-credit second-price auctions. Findings indicate that auction format credibility significantly influences outcomes. While ideal rationality predicts minimal or no shading in credible credit formats and significant shading in non-credit ones, experimental data show substantial shading across both conditions, though significantly less appears when the auction format is genuine. Furthermore, we observe higher levels of shading in non-credit compared to credit scenarios, aligning closely with rational ideal predictions. Notably, auction history played a crucial role: we identified substantial decreases in shading following the public disclosure of bidding data relative to private information conditions. Additionally, most participants displayed decreasing marginal utility based on private valuation findings consistent with previous research.

Neural Painters represent a class of Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) models designed to produce brushstrokes that combine into complete paintings. Although GANs are potent tools for image creation, they present significant challenges in training. Addressing these difficulties, the authors address two specific issues: the diminished fidelity of fine brushstroke details and the protracted training duration. The study introduces two methods to alleviate these problems within the Neural Painters framework. The first, Stroke Clipping, modifies the vectorized stroke representation to filter out unnecessary information prior to encoding, thereby simplifying the input. The second approach, Transfer Learning, is a gain strategy that capitalizes on the GAN's limited capacity by pre-training the encoder and parts of the generator on extensive image datasets. When combined, these techniques accelerate the convergence of the Neural Painter by a factor of five while simultaneously enhancing output quality. The methodology is validated through a comparative analysis of 225 styes created using the trained model. The data can be accessed at: https://www.yanivirshav.com/neural-painters/.

Academic researchers often struggle to locate time to comprehend in-depth scholarly articles. While current Question Answering (QA) tools can handle content delivered via other formats, such as lectures, they fail to address the distinct visual and structural challenges of a paper-based environment. Existing visual QA models concentrate on image analysis but lack specific training on paper layouts, and existing models designed for document QA rely on word-level predictions, which is insufficient for handling images and complex visual structures. To overcome these issues, this study introduces a unified framework for unified document visual question answering, enabling unified processing of visual queries and textual context specific to document layouts. This model predicts unkerstood words within a paper image to answer a given query, utilizing a dedicated image-based QA branch to extract long-range contextual dependencies image-wide, and a language branch to interpret textual queries. This dual approach allows for more efficient visual understanding in paper-based contexts.

We evaluated potential fast flavor instability occurrences in two-state axial-mirror symmetric simulations of the core-collapse of a 25 $M_{\odot}$ star within a 4km $\times$ 4km box. Our simulation box encompasses approximately 8 $\times$ 10$^{15}$ cm$^{-1}$ spherical symmetry, positioned 1 km from the inner boundary. The strong neutrino field generated by the post-shock region exhibits an anisotropic spatial gradient of about 1 km across, with angular variations of order 8 $\times$ 10$^{-2}$ sr from the neutrino source. These conditions yield a collective angular variation parameter exceeding 8 rad, sufficient to trigger fast flavor instability. However, given the lack of significant collective oscillations in the post-shock region due to the absence of sufficient matter density and the dominance of collective angular variation over matter matter effects, fast flavor instability remains absent. Additionally, the collective angular variation parameter is too small to induce fast oscillations at the polar region outside the shock. Consequently, the required conditions for the onset of fast flavor instability remain unmet in this core-collapse scenario.

Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) remains a prevalent yet underdiagnosed condition, prompting extensive research into computerized, data-driven diagnostic systems that rely on neural imaging. Current literature often leverages the spatial resolution of functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data by training deep learning models on the complete brain dataset. This study investigates whether achieving superior generalization for ADHD diagnosis is possible by selecting specific Regions of Interest (RoIs) rather than relying on the entire brain dataset. To address this, we introduce ResDAD, a ResNet-derived architecture trained on selected fMRI brain regions to evaluate performance against models trained on the full dataset. By comparing the two approaches, we assess the utility of focal region training. Empirical results demonstrate that models trained on specific regions outperform those trained on the entire braindataset, yielding a 3.5% increase in classification accuracy for the task. Furthermore, we identified a set of 322 coordinates that align with findings from functional connectivity literature, thereby validating the biological relevance of our selected area strategy. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar123/ResDAD.

Acronyms represent condensed phrases, making their misinterpretation an obstacle to comprehending textual content. While extensive research has addressed acronyms within English texts, many remain uncovered in others, prompting the annotation of 22,255 unique first-acronyms in research papers from ten non-English languages as part of the ACROPER project. These acronyms were then divided into four categories: non-acronyms (entries lacking an initial acronym), multi-acronyms (those with multiple established forms), ambigous-acronyms (those with several relevant applications), and single-acronyms (those with a sole specific meaning). We developed and evaluated base and advanced models for detecting initial acronym occurrences, achieving an English F1 score of 69.66% compared to 75.61% in other languages. Additionally, we integrated domain-specific context features and achieved performance gains of up to 13% across all languages involved.

Quantum interference plays a critical role in the transport properties of electronic devices, such as transistors, which are currently being explored to improve their efficiency. In this research, we investigate the influence of quantum interference on charge and energy transport within a mesoscopic ring mesoscopic system. The ring, constructed from two interconnected onesD graphene nanoribbons, has been analyzed under two distinct magnetic flux conditions: zero and non-zero values, respectively. The findings indicate that at low temperatures, interface defects can suppress quantum interference effects on charge transport but do not significantly impact energy-related currents. However, when interface defects introduce phase shifts, they can enhance quantum interference patterns in the low-temperature thermoelectric charge current. The Seebeck coefficient is observed to exhibit pronounced peaks and minima, with magnitudes that fluctuate non-monotonically with respect to the phase shift.

We introduce a new DNA-storage architecture that enables rapid, localized updates—a capability absent in previous approaches where data is typically fragmented into fixed fragments mapped to specific storage locations. In our proposed solution, original data is divided into variable-sized fragments, with each encoded using a unique identifier. These fragments are then stored in fixed locations, which currently remain the primary challenge. To facilitate targeted modifications later, we employ channel coding specifically designed for the unstable (erasure-prone) conditions typical of DNA memory. This strategy allows the physical location of a data fragment to update without necessitating a total rewrite of that specific fragment, including its original content. Additionally, we demonstrate that this method supports localized retrieval, significantly enhancing readout efficiency. Our simulation results indicate a data expansion of up to an order of magnitude compared to prior schemes.

Topological insulators are distinguished by their distinct transport characteristics, specifically the interplay between time-reversal symmetry, surface states, and Dirac cones. However, practical transport measurements often struggle to isolate signatures unique to topological insulators due to competing bulk effects and complicated surface states. In this study, we examine the Hall effect and the anomalous Hall effect in the doped topological insulator, $\text{Bi}_{2}\text{Te}_{3}$, utilizing a novel method: angular-resolved Hall measurement. By measuring Hall resistivity across different in-plane orientations, we identify minima corresponding to the crystal direction. At these points, bulk contributions vanish, enabling the direct experimental observation of the anomalous Hall effect. Furthermore, we present a model that relates these experimental observations to surface conductivity, offering clear evidence for the dominance of the surface anomaly in doping-related topological insulators, $\text{Bi}_{2}\text{Te}_{3}$.

In a medium capable of oscillation, a localized source known as a pacemaker consistently emits waves. When this medium and its waves are periodic, varying frequencies at the source can influence the state of oscillation across the entire system. This research examines the interaction between these waves and the medium's reactive phase, specifically exploring the influence of emitted frequencies and injected power on: (i) the propagation speed of the waves, (ii) the level of desynchrononization within a ring-shaped domain, and (iii) the exclusion of local synchronization within a three-dimensional spherical medium. These computational findings align well with visual experimental outcomes. Furthermore, the study outlines how the medium's intrinsic period can (dis)synchronize an injected pacemaker and the associated wave dynamics.

Entropy serves as a fundamental concept in probability theory and probability distributions. This paper introduces quantum algorithms that estimate von Neumann and Shannon entropies, as well as generalizations such as R\'enyi and Tsallis entropies. The algorithms are underpinned by two distinct quantum frameworks: (1) an "informed" approach, and (2) a unitary method operating on unit entropy-encoded quantum states. Notably, the second approach does not require a pre-knowledge of the probability distribution. Additionally, the paper presents a new algorithm specifically for estimating the trace distance between two unit entropy-encoded quantum states.

Deep Learning and AI models depend heavily on massive datasets for effective training, validation, and testing. Establishing these datasets demands intricate, time-intensive processes that necessitate significant human expertise and effort. Consequently, there is an urgent need for solutions that facilitate the generation and management of such data. This study introduces a novel approach for automatically creating and validating diverse benchmarks for computer vision by leveraging large-scale text corpora. By extracting visual concepts from text to define benchmark definitions, our method also develops corresponding visual benchmarks to assess them. We outline the essential steps and underlying concepts for establishing both textual and visual benchmarks, providing examples to illustrate their application. Furthermore, to support the creation of visual benchmarks, a new model named T2Image has been devised; it utilizes a dual-encoder architecture to map textual inputs into unique four-dimensional visual codes. We evaluate T2Image's capabilities against established visual benchmarks and existing methods, showing that it produces distinct benchmarks with unique characteristics. This breakthrough opens new avenues for generating novel AI and computer vision benchmarks from large language models, delivering distinct datasets for training, validating, and testing.

Clinical text notes offer rich, informative content that could aid in assigning ICD codes to ICDS revisions. Nevertheless, extracting these specific diagnoses from unstructured text poses significant challenges, thereby hindering the use of such records for funding and performance metrics in clinical and administrative settings. To address this, we introduce DistILated Encoder (DE), a novel BERT-based framework that distills knowledge. DE was trained on 209,000 records containing both clinical text and ICD-10-CM assignments, achieving a Macro F1 score of 0.6025. When compared to state-of-the-art ensemble models, DE delivers a 2.3% improvement in performance while consuming only a fraction of the computational resources.

Let $R = k[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ be the polynomial ring with $n$ variables, where the scalar field is $k$. For a monomial ideal, we define an almost Cohen-Macaulay (ACM) simplicial complex as one that is Cohen-Macaulay after adding a single generator, which itself has a degree no lower than $n$. In addition, we define an ACM face ring as one where the Cohen-Macaulay property is achieved by adding only two generators of degree at most $n$. This paper characterizes ACM monomial ideals and their corresponding simplicial complexes by providing necessary and sufficient conditions. We further classify these ideals and complexes based on their Gorenstein properties, Borel triangulation, and squarefree monomial ideals.

Machine Learning (ML) algorithms are capable of uncovering profound insights from extensive datasets, yet the growing volume of data threatens to impede their practical utility. Quantum computing presents a transformative avenue for ML by enhancing the efficiency of data processing. This research examines various quantum machine learning (QML) approaches alongside their corresponding classical counterparts. The analysis begins with quantum algorithms for linear algebra, a foundation crucial for many ML tasks, followed by an exploration specific applications such as the quantum algorithm for the linear support vector classifier and its adaptation across different qubit systems. Finally, we assess the current state of QML by highlighting pivotal milestones in advancement, the entrenched obstacles restricting widespread adoption, and the most promising future trajectories for the field.

This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of prime-field microlensing planetary events, focusing on those discovered by the KMTNet and planned to be monitored by LMA. Event OYIT-2018-GL1, identified in a previous study, is a clear example of such a case. By applying high-resolution imaging, we obtained high-quality light curves for three additional events: OYIT-2019-BM1, OYIT-2020-AL1, and OYIT-2017-ER1. For each event, we developed microlensing models, with OYIT-2018-GL1 being the sole multi-planetary system confirmed. Our analysis yields lens mass estimates within an order of magnitude accuracy for all four cases, with the two events that exhibited clear planetary signatures having masses around several times Jupiter's mass. Statistical evaluation of these prime-field candidates provides robust mass function estimates while highlighting the critical importance of ongoing monitoring. Furthermore, we outline the characteristics and benefits of utilizing high-acuity prime-field microlensing events, demonstrating their significant potential for identifying high-mass ratio systems and precisely constraining planet mass functions.

Increasing attention is focused on image-based inverse problems, particularly for recovering depth maps. This paper presents a differentiable renderer, applicable to inverse problems in general, solved using gradient descent. The approach differentiates every step, from ray generation to anti-aliasing compositing. Anti-aliasing is handled using two techniques: pre-computing with a high sampling rate, or analytically determining the renderer's differentiability during the composition process. This paper focuses primarily on the analytical method. While the proposed differentiable strategy can be rendered pre-computed, this paper shows an even greater advantage with on-the-fly computation. This allows the method to adapt the ray distribution to specific areas of interest. This paper shows that the proposed method can be used to solve various image-related inverse problems, such as reflectance factorization.

Current network traffic models utilize various data sources, such as GPS data from navigation apps and toll transactions, to estimate flow. While GPS provides valuable insights, this data is dispersed and carries significant variability in estimated traffic between different locations. This study presents a stochastic traffic model that integrates flow estimation techniques with traffic flow estimation and employs a Variance Reduction Method to enhance traditional estimation methods. This new approach is evaluated using both synthetic and real-world data.

We analyze finite lattices composed of nonlinear autonomous oscillators coupled by nearest-neighbor interactions, featuring purely conservative coupling and random quenched frequencies. Using numerical simulations, we examine how global synchronization breaks down upon varying system parameters. We observe that as parameters are changed, the synchronized state becomes unstable with the advent of localized periodic and chaotic behaviors; weak nonlinear nonlinearities govern the transition from complete synchrony to this localized periodic regime. Furthermore, we evaluate the fraction of initial conditions that lead to synchronized trajectories as a function of parameter changes. Finally, we extend our findings from systems with conservative coupling to those involving dissipation and external periodic driving forces.

This note compares Wilson's algorithm and Peps's treepipe algorithm, both of which construct uniform spanning trees from rooted graphs using random walks and a fixed boundary. It is demonstrated that treepipe operates as a specialized instance of Wilson's algorithm, with both methods relying on the concept of a "frozen boundary." In this context, the frozen boundary acts as a substitute for the standard condition and is depicted as evolving over time alongside the random walk, rather than remaining static. The findings also highlight that the algorithms differ in their treatment of the frozen boundary: treepipe expands it concurrently with the exploration, whereas Wilson's algorithm delays its expansion until specific instances. It is proven that the tuning of Wilson's algorithm can support simultaneous proof of two related results: the first shows that for any graph, a tree exists connecting the roots to the frozen boundary, and the second shows that when starting from a larger starting configuration, the algorithm successfully connects the exploration to a smaller, contained frozen boundary.

A primary challenge in consuming Linked Data involves designing visual and natural language interfaces accessible to non-technical users. Using ontodia combined with the Wikidata set in this paper, this paper explores diagrammatic data analysis and introduces advances to the system's text-based query capabilities for exploring Linked Data elements. Our approach employs distributional semantics-based models, paired with different types of word embeddings, to discover and prioritize entity traits in response to user inputs. Tests conducted with subject matter experts using diatheon showed that the proposed methods effectively support exploration, with query accuracy increasing as the linguistic distance of the target feature words increases.

Black solitons found within intensity-dependent dispersion variants of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which operates under N₁ > N₂ > 0 conditions and exhibits N₁ > N₂ > 0, are examined for stability. A novel approach to analyzing their stability is presented. First, a complex coordinate system is defined; within this framework, the N1, N2, N3 equation is reduced to a pair of coupled real nonlinear ordinary differential equations. This reduction yields a simplified version of the standard black soliton, now dependent on soliton intensity. This modified intensity-dependent dispersion-dependent structure fundamentally alters the underlying ordinary differential equations. Furthermore, this phenomenon influences the specific location where the derivative of the soliton function vanishes. Ultimately, this modification yields a novel type of stability criterion for black soliton solutions.

This paper introduces a co-adaptive guidance framework for visual analytics that streamlines the arduous process of iterative refinement in both human-centric and machine-centric strategies. Through iterative cycles, experts identify enhancements to improve system performance, yet this tradition often imposes a significant time burden. Our framework applies transfer learning to propagate insights from seasoned professionals to novices, effectively communicating established improvements through two mechanisms: automated, system-driven recommendations and user-adaptive suggestions. The latter tailor suggestions specifically to individual user behaviors, facilitating personalized system evolution. We validated this approach on a medical dataset, establishing a user model to investigate individual differences in visual analysis patterns. Our results indicate that co-adaptive guidance successfully accelerates the co-adaptation process, enabling users to achieve performance levels comparable to those of experts.

This study outlines an approach for engineering stellarators with enhanced global performance through achieved quasisymmetry. Achieving this goal demands that the integrated quantities which cause key quasisymmetric observables to disappear be meticulously minimized. The method involves a specific class of quantities termed "localqs," defined by their ability to evaluate directly from particle orbits. We introduce a framework to derive expressions for these localqs arising from both magnetic well-shaped and curvature scalar effects. The framework is then applied to a simplified, analytic magnetic field model with up to eightfold rotational symmetry. In this scenario, we determine the actual localqs, comparing them against approximations based on local magnetic field strength. The results demonstrate a significant reduction in our computed localqs relative to the standing international stellarator benchmarks, specifically from the LSX project.

Effective temperature control in catalytic fixed bed reactors is vital for ensuring process safety and optimizing catalytic performance. This study investigates one-dimensional steady-state heat and mass transfer within a fixed bed to develop a novel analytical method for the exact solution of temperature and concentration profiles, applicable even when reaction rates exhibit exponential temperature dependencies. A unique weighted function transformation is employed to linearize the governing ordinary differential equations, followed by solutions expressed through variation of parameters, Frobenius series, or Bessel functions, or a combination thereof. To handle singular points, Frobenius series solutions are specifically utilized. The proposed methodologies are validated via numerical examples, and the resulting general formulas are combined using a power series approach with whole numbers to formulate polynomial-type reaction rate functions.

Biomolecular condensates form spontaneously within the dense cellular environment when proteins and nucleic acids demix into protein-rich and protein-poor phases, a process driven by weak multivalent interactions. This study introduces a theoretical framework to calculate the phase diagram, which accounts for the diverse sizes and concentrations of various molecular types found in cells, as well as their polydispersity. Our approach integrates concepts from multicomponent fluid thermodynamics with statistical mechanics models of multivalent interactions to introduce components with different interaction strengths, average valencies, and size distributions. We determine average interaction forces between molecules of different types and derive mean-field free-energies that include entropic factors arising from mixing, volume exclusion, and the distribution of molecular sizes and valencies. Finally, we apply these theoretical results to simulate how adding different molecules alters the phase behavior of proteins and their sensitivity regarding concentration thresholds and size variations.

This study examines the rotation of both magnetic and observational features within sunspot regions during a solar flare on April 24, 2007, marked by an X1.1 event. Data derived from Ca II H spectral images captured with a Ca II 3873 Å narrow-band imaging system at Kitt Peak National Solar Observatory reveal the pre-flare state of the spot. Post-flare rotation speeds were quantified using pixel-based cross-correlation on multi-wavelength images (405 nm, 501.6 nm, and 630 nm) obtained from NSO's Diamond Jubilee Solar Telescope. Results indicate that the magnetic main flux tubes rotate faster than their observational counterparts and the solar surface. The sunspot's northern delta spot displayed opposite rotational directions for its magnetic north and south substructures relative to the solar surface; the western side of the delta rotated more rapidly than its eastern counterpart. Furthermore, magnetic components exhibited rotation rates approximately 10% higher than observational ones across all bands. The study concludes by suggesting models for the rotational divergence of delta spot magnetic components and the variance in rotational speeds between magnetic East-West segments.

This note introduces and analyzes the $b$-principle concerning oriented colored broken submersions (OCBS), demonstrating that every such map is equivalent to a submersion under the appropriate conditions within the homotopy category. Consequently, the note establishes a $b$-principle for these structures. This principle relates oriented colored broken submersions on a given manifold $M$ to section spaces of a specific fiber bundle.

This study evaluates the arithmetic complexity and efficiency of two nested-Bianchi-inertial wrappers (NBI)—specifically, a scalar and a block variant—applied to a linearized, large deformation mechanical behavior model of the heart. These wrappers represent a class of preconditoner that enhance multigrid solver performance; they are constructed by aggregating linear predictions over subdomains to approximate the global stiffness matrix more adaptively. To support our analysis, we applied these wrappers within a parallel multigrid framework on an anatomical heart structure, solving a case involving coupled electomechanical problems. Our observations indicate that both versions outperform a standard NBI preconditoner in reducing time steps required for convergence. Notably, the block NBI demonstrates superior arithmetic handling and maintains high efficiency across expanding mesh coarsening in periodic directions, making it particularly well-suited for partitioned domain decompositions. This conclusion aligns with theoretical expectations and underscores the wrapper's value in cardiac mechanical simulations.

User-generated content, primarily in the form of tags, has proliferated across the web, creating a need for enhanced understanding of tagging systems and the development of novel analytical algorithms. In this paper, we introduce insights derived from our comprehensive study of millions of real-world tags extracted from both YouTube and Flickr. We examine fundamental characteristics such as tag, user, and topic distributions, alongside a detailed exploration of co-occurrence patterns, suggestive behaviors, and organizational efforts. Leveraging these large-scale datasets, we have constructed and released the Flickr 200M co-occurring Tag dataset, enabling the study of individual and collective suggesting, as well as formal topic modeling. Moreover, we have released extensive data regarding Youtubers' and Flickr contributors' tags along with their network interactions. All sourced materials are publicly available at http://research.google.com/projects/labs-ysu/amilliontags/.

The emergence of bianisotropic acoustic metagrids marks a significant advancement, opening new possibilities for wave manipulation in applications such as ultrasound imaging and medical therapy. This study presents the first experimental verification of a bianisotropic acoustic metagrant featuring both linear and nonlinear electromagnetic-like gyroscopic properties. Operating in the ultrasonic frequency range, the device relies on a rigid plastic structure etched with pin-sized holes arranged on a honeycomb lattice. Both positive and negative refraction, as well as harmonic generation, were observed during 1D scanning normal to the surface, which correspond to diagonal and off-diagonal Hall effects. Furthermore, angular dependence measurements revealed noise-free acoustical Lorentz forces. These outcomes confirm that complex acoustic interactions can be engineered by exploiting diagonal (gyro) and off-diagonal (magnetoresistance) effective properties within passive acoustic systems.

This paper investigates the long-term asymptotics of the strong solutions for the 2-D FENE dumbbell model. By utilizing the Gronwall inequality alongside the properties of the 2-D hydrodynamic Stokes operator, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ norm decays exponentially over time. Furthermore, we examine how the higher-order $H^m$ norms ($m \geq 1$) decay as time progresses towards the large scale.

System-level evaluation is essential to determine the potential of IAB, which can be achieved using a mobility, topology, and mobility model. The standard IAB model is first expanded to distinguish between fully connected and partially connected nodes. The distribution of child nodes is then described using an inhomogeneous Cox process, with their link counts modeled by a Poisson distribution. The density function is solved using an adaptive density approach that considers both direct and indirect connections. Although reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in controlled environments, such as gaming, transferring these techniques to open-world scenarios presents distinct challenges. The primary obstacle is RL's tendency to converge on local optima, generating repetitive behaviors that often fail to discover more rewarding actions. Standard methods offering only partial or no rewards struggle in complex settings, where the meaningful reward may remain elusive for extended periods, causing agents to ignore potential high-value goals. This paper introduces a new RL approach that mitigates these convergence issues by integrating world embeddings with attention mechanisms. By having agents receive frequent, immediate feedback and by allowing them to prioritize specific task sub-components within an embedding that captures the world state, this architecture guides the search toward higher rewards more effectively. Experimental results across diverse simulations demonstrate that this attention-based RL scheme surpasses current benchmarks in partial reward scenarios, including *Among Us*, a text-based "Find the Cat" application, and a financial trading benchmark.

Liger is a Liger-III class integral field spectrograph designed for the 400-820 nm wavelength range, developed for the 4-m William Herschel Telescope to provide high-resolution data (R = 2,000–7,000) for both Galactic and Galactic-centric studies. This paper provides details on the instrument's design, commissioning, and performance metrics, including initial observations. As a body rotation spectrograph, Liger utilizes an 11-plane slicer and a 7-microlens array, directing stellar fields up to 1.5 arcminutes in size to a V-photometric single-mode fiber. Light from the fiber is then collimated, passed through a slicer, and directed onto an 8k x 8k MOSAIC II CCD detector. Each slice is subsequently dispersed by a triple grating system to the slicer's complementary 4k x 4k CCD. Initial commissioning yielded excellent results with slice dispersion reaching 112 micropixels per arcsecond, slice-to-slice variations below 1.5%, slice contrast under 1%, and slit loss less than 15%.

This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H₂ equation through a correspondence involving linear relations paired with Cauchy matrix matrices. We demonstrate that this equation describes the discrete temporal evolution of specific entry constraints within an associated Cauchy matrix, governed by a Lax pair pair of differential equations. Last, we show that both the Toda lattice and discrete Burgers equation can be expressed as special limits or cases of the H₂ model.

This paper examines the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection during the inference phase, despite the model's capacity to identify these false positives within its own training data. The authors posit that the root cause lies in the training process, which, to ensure a stable gradient and efficient convergence during multi-task learning, discards prediction scores lower than the current loss value before they can contribute to the final decision. This suppression leads the model to overlook and thus fail to detect actual relationship instances. To address this, this study proposes VRI-ViT, which integrates Vision Transformers into a VRI-ViT framework. This new architecture allows the model to access its intrinsic capacity for predicting the specific value score at any step of training, enabling it to make a final decision based on that score even if it results in slower convergence. Empirically, this method maintains a stable training process, matches the performance of prior state-of-the-art models, and achieves a significant 30% reduction in errors.

This study examines the correlation between quantum cost-correlation (QCC) and trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) using a two-qubit $\otimes$ two-qubit system. We conduct a comparative analysis of weak-measurement effects on TQD and QCC, specifically within a bipartite configuration. Our analysis, focused on a weakly coupled isolated two-qubit doublet system, involves tracing out interactions with the environment and applying local weak-measurement operations. We calculate both TQD and QCC under these conditions and analyze their dependence on the weak-strength parameter of the measurement. We observe that both quantities initially decline before eventually stabilizing. Notably, we found that the QCC decreases at a more rapid rate compared to TQD. Furthermore, we performed a detailed investigation into how a quantum trajectory-based weak-strength parameter influences these measurements and their response to various initial quantum states.

This study investigates the cosmological radio constraints on primordial black hole (PBH) scenarios where dark matter (DM) is entirely composed of PBHs. We calculate the expected radio brightness temperature ($T_b$) from the Pop III star epoch and from Hawking radiation emitted by PBHs. The Pop III contribution remains negligible against existing upper limits derived from PBH models. Conversely, the induced $T_b$ from complete evaporation is $10^{-14} \text{ K}$, falling far below current constraints. However, if PBHs possess charges, the resulting emission is substantially boosted; we determine the maximum allowable charge for PBH-only dark matter to remain invisible to radio surveys. The strictest limit applies to the electron-positron charge range ($10^{-1}-10^{0}e$), excluding such charged PBHs from constituting the entire dark matter population.

We introduce FHC, an end-to-end protocol for secure cloud computation based on Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). In this framework, a client can securely outsource data to the cloud, allowing a server to execute operations on encrypted data without ever exposing it. Clients retain control by retrieving the final encrypted result and decrypting it locally.

While this ensures privacy, standard FHE schemes typically suffer from significant performance overhead. To address this, we propose two key innovations. First, we develop an efficient data compression scheme that reduces memory footprint and communication costs by leveraging predictive encoding for time series data. Second, we optimize cloud operations by substituting direct FHE computations with a hybrid approach that integrates standard encryption with Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). This strategy enables the efficient handling of large-scale integer additions and multiplication on the encrypted data.

Experimental evaluations using both real-world datasets and synthetically generated data confirm that our approach delivers substantial gains. We observed speed improvements of 2 to three orders of magnitude and memory savings of a factor of 100 compared to conventional FHE implementations.
